utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will deal with the first three grounds of appeal concerning criminal responsibility. In each of these grounds, the Prosecution focuses primarily on errors of omission, where the Trial Chamber leaves something incompletely adjudicated. I will then hand over to my colleague Ms. Goy, who will address ground 4 on sentencing. Starting with ground 1, which raises five interrelated errors in the Trial Chamber's JCE analysis. I'd like to jump first to the heart of ground 1, the failure to adjudicate or give reasons, which is subground 1(c). The problem here is a very simple one. In relation to many of the JCE incidents, the Trial Chamber did not adjudicate individual criminal responsibility for these crimes in any meaningful way. The Trial Chamber assesses the evidence and finds that the crimes charged in the indictment were factually proven beyond a reasonable doubt, and that's generally found in volume 2 or the beginnings of volume 3. And then the Chamber finds that the alleged incidents meet all of the legal elements of the crimes charged in volume 3, and the Trial Chamber goes on to find that the crimes were the "natural and foreseeable consequence of the JCE 1 being carried out." Volume 4, paragraph 72. The Chamber diligently made all these findings. However, when it comes to who should be held criminally responsible, the Trial Chamber fails to systematically address whether each of the defendants could personally foresee the risk that each of these proven criminal incidents might occur. And to the extent that this failure to adjudicate was an implicit acquittal, in the sense that no conviction was entered, the Prosecution has also appealed this as a failure to give reasons. I should point out at the outset that for Pusic these crimes are technically adjudicated, but they're all adjudicated in one single sentence. Volume 4, paragraph 1216. The Chamber gives a sweeping omnibus dismissal of all but two of the JCE 3 incidents. Without assessing the evidence, the Chamber just says that it does not have any evidence of his JCE 3 guilt. This bare adjudication for Pusic is appealed only as a failure to give a reasoned opinion. So, Your Honours, let me take you to one example to illustrate the nature of this problem. In paragraph 161 of the indictment, the Prosecution charges all six of the accused with the murder of Sanida Kaplan in Stolac on 13 July 1993. Her name is specified in the indictment's annex. Sanida was killed after HVO armed forces entered her tiny village, which consisted of only 13 Muslim and two Croat houses. She was just shy of her 18th birthday. The HVO forces came into the village and they proceeded to violently expel the Muslim families from their homes. They arrested the men who had not been rounded up in previous raids, firing weapons and shouting death threats. In the course of these expulsions, an HVO soldier named Dragan Bonojza arrived at the front door of the Kaplan home. As Sanida came to her front door, he opened fire at close range, killing her in a burst of gun-fire. Her mother Fata watched helplessly as her daughter was shot in the head. She testified before this Tribunal that the killer then forced her to leave her daughter's body. Along with her neighbours and the rest of her family, Fata was then taken away by the HVO and detained in a school in a nearby village. The Chamber's findings on these facts can be found at volume 2, paragraphs 1934 to 1938. The Chamber went on to find that Sanida Kaplan's killing was both a murder as a crime against humanity charged under Count 2 and wilful killing of a civilian charged as Count 3. And that's volume 3, paragraphs 684 and 735. The Chamber found that in order to evict Muslims from their homes in furtherance of the common criminal purpose, the HVO forces engaged in acts of extreme violence, threatening and mistreating Muslims, making such killings and other crimes a natural and foreseeable consequence of the joint criminal enterprise. That's volume 4, paragraph 72. At volume 4, paragraphs 70, the Trial Chamber even lists this exact killing as an example of the foreseeable JCE 3 crimes. Despite having made all of these specific findings about this killing: that it happened as charged, who did it, that it was an international crime, and even what mode of liability should apply, the Chamber fails to determine if three of the six accused were criminally responsible. It only addresses the criminal responsibility of Petkovic and Coric. And for Pusic, this incident is one of the 33 dismissed without any reasons. And this is not the only murder that was overlooked. In fact, the Trial Chamber does not address whether Stojic or Praljak could foresee any of the 53 murders under JCE 3. Fifty-three people were found to have been murdered in the execution of the joint criminal enterprise, and the Chamber didn't even consider whether Stojic or Praljak were responsible for any of them. And the Chamber fails to address the criminal responsibility of any of the defendants for any of the identified crimes in Prozor municipality under JCE 3. None of the Prozor murders, none of the rapes or sexual assaults, not the destruction of the Skrobucani mosque, and not the thefts. And the Chamber missed other entire municipalities of crimes in relation to other defendants. And when Your Honours exam this issue more closely, you will see that the Chamber's treatment is inexplicably inconsistent across the six defendants. So to give you a sense of the scale of this problem -- I'm hoping it will come up on the big screen. To give you a sense of the scale of the problem, so based on indictment and the trial judgement that we've summarised in the tables in our appeals brief, there were approximately 36 JCE 3 incidents. And I would note that each incident might comprise more than one victim or occur over a period of time. So you multiply this by six accused. And if you adjust a bit for those who joined the JCE later or left earlier, there's a total of approximately of 211 incidents for which we would expect the Trial Chamber to address criminal responsibility. And the circle represents these 200 expected criminal responsibility adjudications. Of the 211, around 150 of them are missing. So this is the orange piece of the pie. Either the Chamber did not address criminal responsibility at all or, for Pusic, dismissed the 33 incidents in a single unreferenced sentence. So for more than 70 per cent of the proven JCE 3 incidents, we do not have a finding on individual criminal responsibility or at least not reasoned ones. The scale of this omission is unprecedented and it cannot stand. The Trial Chamber appears to have forgotten to determine which of the defendants bears criminal responsibility for these serious crimes against humanity and war crimes. And this is an unacceptable outcome for everyone, for the victims; for the witnesses, such as Fata Kaplan, the bereaved mother who travelled to The Hague to tell the Chamber -- to tell this Court about her daughter's murder and her family's ordeal. And it's an unacceptable outcome for the international community and for the legacy of this Court. It's the primary responsibility of the Trial Chamber to fully adjudicate the indictment before it, and in this case justice has been left incomplete. Your Honours, I will turn now to the grounds of appeal that concern the JCE 3 incidents that were adjudicated by the Trial Chamber. Starting with ground 1(a), this is the mens rea error. In short, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber erred in applying the wrong mental element for JCE 3. The correct standard is whether the foreseeable crimes were a possible consequence of the joint criminal enterprise. According to the well-established case law, this test is not satisfied by implausibly remote scenarios. The law requires that the possibility that a crime might be committed is sufficiently substantial to be foreseeable to the accused. And I'd refer Your Honours to Sainovic appeals judgement, paragraph 1557; and the Karadzic JCE 3 appeals decision cited in our brief. But in this case, in many instances, the Trial Chamber looked for a probable rather than a possible consequence that the crimes would be committed instead of could or might and that the crimes were a probable outcome of the furtherance of the common purpose instead of a possible one. And this sets the level of foreseeability too high. Your Honours, because the original language of the trial judgement is French, I'm putting both the original and the translation of the paragraphs that I'll be citing up on the screen. And you can see that in volume 1, paragraph 216, the Chamber sets the legal standard for JCE 3 too high. The Chamber says that the JCE 3 requires that the accused deliberately assumed the risk that the crime would be committed, because he knew that a crime of this sort was the probable outcome of the furtherance of the common criminal purpose. The Trial Chamber applied this heightened standard in many places throughout its JCE 3 analysis. And the Trial Chamber's analysis of Stojic's criminal responsibility is a good example of this error in action, because the Trial Chamber uses the heightened standard consistently in its analysis. So starting at volume 4, paragraph 433, the Trial Chamber sets out to assess whether Stojic could reasonably have foreseen that the JCE 3 crimes would be committed and took that risk. The Trial Chamber then consistently applies the wrong standard to all nine of its findings. Applying the wrong standard, it convicts Stojic of five JCE 3 crimes. At paragraph 437 it reasoned that he could foresee -- could have foreseen that HVO members would also commit sexual abuse during the Mostar evictions. And at paragraphs 439, 445, 446, and 447, that he could foresee HVO would commit acts of theft. And then applying the wrong standard again, the Trial Chamber acquits him of four crimes, finding at paragraphs 441, 443, 448, and 449 of volume 4, that he could not have foreseen that thefts or religious destruction would occur during certain operations. The Trial Chamber is not consistent. In some places, most notably in its analysis of Prlic's responsibility, the Trial Chamber refers to the correct level of foreseeability, a possibility. But in relation to the majority of the adjudicated JCE 3 crimes, the Trial Chamber applies the incorrect probability standard. The heightened legal standard results in erroneous acquittals in relation to 21 incidents. To the extent that Pusic's omnibus acquittal was an adjudication, it also seems to have been done at this heightened standard, raising the total number of errors to 54. These are the incidents that the Prosecution has appealed. For ten additional incidents, the foreseeability evidence was so strong that the Trial Chamber convicted at the heightened standard. And let me pause here because this is the subject matter of question 10 from the Bench. Your Honours, even though there is a legal error in the existing -- in some of the existing JCE 3 convictions, it is not one that invalidates the judgement. The evidence that satisfies the higher standard probability would necessarily also satisfy the correct standard. Neither the Prosecution nor the Defence have appealed these legal errors because they have no impact. Applying the correct test, the outcome is the same: Conviction. Various respondents have suggested in their briefs that the Trial Chamber should be presumed to have applied the correct test despite its choice of language. But, Your Honours, this is not a case where the Chamber deliberately sets out to analyse the facts against the correct legal standard and then uses a couple of stray words. Here, the Chamber sets out the law at the wrong standard and then actively refers to this wrong standard in approximately 75 per cent of the JCE 3 crimes it adjudicates. For only 14 of the 60 adjudicated JCE 3 incidents does it appear that the Chamber applied the correct standard, so there's no basis to presume that the correct test was applied. Your Honours, we ask that you apply the correct standard to the Chamber's findings in the evidence and convict the respondents as set out in our brief. Turning now to ground 1(b) concerning the compartmentalisation of the evidence. Your Honours, in this ground, in this subground, the Prosecution takes issue with the Chamber's restrictive assessment of the evidence related to foreseeability. In assessing whether the JCE 3 crimes were foreseeable, the Trial Chamber was, of course, required to look at the totality of the evidence, including the surrounding circumstances in which the crimes were committed. And the totality of the accused's relevant intent and knowledge. Instead, it focussed very narrowly on the particular location under consideration, assessing whether a particular crime was foreseeable based exclusively on events in and information about that particular municipality, village, or detention centre. I will illustrate this compartmentalisation error with a simple example. When considering Prlic's JCE 3 responsibility for the 5 December 1993 shooting death of a detainees in the Vojno detention centre, the Trial Chamber found that Prlic was only informed of the killings in that location by an ICRC letter on 20 January 1994, just over a month later. It reasoned that since the crime occurred before he received the letter, it couldn't find that he could reasonably have foreseen the murder. That's at volume 4, paragraph 287. But the Chamber erred in focussing exclusively on this one ICRC letter as the exclusive evidence of the foreseeability of this killing. Based on this piece of evidence, assessed in isolation, the Trial Chamber acquitted; and that was wrong. In order to properly assess whether Prlic could foresee the risk that a murder might occur in Vojno detention facility in December 1993 many months into the execution of the joint criminal enterprise, the Trial Chamber was required to look beyond actual notice of murders in that particular location. And if it had done so, it is clear from the Chamber's other findings that by December 1993 Prlic could foresee the risk that murders of Muslims might occur in the HVO network of detention facilities, including at Vojno. So, for example, it would have been relevant to the Chamber's assessment that the JCE -- that the Trial Chamber concluded that Prlic could foresee murders in other detention facilities in the same network, for example, in Sovici and Doljani, as early as April 1993. That's volume 4, paragraph 283. And that Prlic knew of the life-threatening conditions in two other network detention facilities, Dretelj and Gabela by 19th of July, 1993. Volume 4 paragraph 286. And that Prlic could foresee other murders during evictions from at least June 1993. Volume 4, paragraph 284. And let's not forget that the Chamber's JCE 1 finding that Prlic shared the intent to remove the Muslim population from Herceg-Bosna through commission of crimes, including persecution and murder. Volume 4, paragraph 276 and 287. That he shared the intent to detain Muslims in cruel and inhuman conditions and to mistreat them and to use them for forced labour resulting in their death on the front line. Volume 4, paragraph 23 -- sorry, 273, 274, and 287. Had the Trial Chamber not made a legal error in looking only at that Vojno evidence in isolation, the only conclusion available on the totality of the evidence was that Prlic was aware of the possibility that a Vojno detainee might be killed in December 1993, and he should be convicted under JCE 3 for this crime. As set out in our brief, this error - artificially compartmentalising the evidence in this way - has resulted in and contributed to erroneous acquittals. And we ask Your Honours to correct these errors as set out in our brief. In relation to Coric, the Trial Chamber took this compartmentalisation to the extreme. This is subground 1(d). The Trial Chamber not only limited its evidentiary analysis to a specific location, it also required that Coric contributed to a particular JCE 1 crime in those locations as a precondition for JCE 3 responsibility. The Trial Chamber was not even satisfied that Coric participated in related JCE 1 crimes in those same localities. So the Chamber found that Coric participated in the arrest and detention of the men in Stolac and Capljina, but because he did not personally have a hand in the concurrent evictions of the women, children, and elderly, the Chamber found that he was not responsible for those JCE 3 crimes, which included 16 murders including Sanida Kaplan and the thefts. And that's volume 4, paragraph 1015, referring back to paragraph 953. In doing so, the Trial Chamber adds a new requirement that the accused must have specifically contributed to a particular JCE 1 crime in a particular location, and this is an error. There's no legal basis for this additional requirement. Indeed, any such requirement would run contrary to the very foundation of the legal notion of joint criminal enterprise, which is based on participants contributing to different activities in order to achieve their shared common criminal purpose. Finally, Your Honours, in ground 1(e), the Prosecution also raises errors of fact. No reasonable trier of fact could have acquitted for these crimes. For the detailed factual arguments in relation to each respondent, we rely on the submissions set out in our briefs. It suffices for my oral submissions to point out that correcting these errors would not require extensive appellant fact-finding. Applying the correct legal and evidentiary standards, the respondents' convictions for JCE 3 responsibility in most instances can be entered based on the Chamber's own findings. In particular, Your Honours, the Chamber has already made findings on many of the contextual factors that the Appeals Chamber has previously identified as making the commission of a specific type of crime falling outside the common purpose foreseeable. And I'd refer Your Honours to Sainovic appeals judgement paragraph 1089. For example, the Trial Chamber found that each of the JCE members intended a wide range of violent and persecutory crimes against Muslims - these were the means by which the common purpose was to be achieved - and not just for forcible displacement crimes, but also murders during attacks and the wanton and extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity. They intended illegal detentions and the inhuman and cruel treatment of vulnerable detainees and murders during dangerous and illegal front line forced labour. And after (sic) 30 June 1993, the JCE members were found to have intended to spread terror, to unlawfully attack Muslim civilians through sniping and shelling, to destroy Muslim religious buildings. And it's not only their intent to further the common criminal purpose using incredibly violent means, they were each also aware of how the JCE was being implemented on the ground. The JCE members knew that eviction operations involved a climate of extreme violence. There are many findings in the judgement on this. Each of them was aware of the climate of ethnic animosity, ethnic separation was their very purpose. Each of them participated in various aspects of the pattern of criminality in execution of the joint criminal enterprise across different municipalities and in various detention settings. And they and their fellow JCE members were not taking any -- or at least not any effective steps to curb this criminality, further fuelling the possibility that it would occur again and again in the course of the JCE's implementation across Herceg-Bosna. And each of them were aware of factors identified in previous cases as making victims more vulnerable, thereby indicating a heightened risk of JCE 3 crimes. For example, they knew about separations based on gender, that the male Muslim population was being rounded up and detained, separating them from the women, children, and the elderly. Each of them knew that detainees were being held in terrible conditions where they were subjected to deprivations and violence. And they knew of the presence of criminals in units dispatched to carry out operations in close contact with Muslim civilians, such as Naletilic's notorious convicts battalion. The Chamber's compartmentalised assessment of JCE 3 crimes fails to address this overall context. But when you break down the compartments and put the Chamber's factual findings back together, in most instances this is already sufficient, sufficient to demonstrate beyond a reasonable doubt that each of the respondents could foresee the risk that murders, rapes, destruction of religious property, and thefts might occur. As an example, look at the Chamber's assessment of the foreseeability of thefts, plunder and appropriation of property. The Chamber found that all five of the defendants who were JCE members at that time could foresee JCE 3 threats following the attacks on Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. So from the very beginning of the JCE's implementation, each of them already knew that eviction operations were being conducted in a manner that made threats a possible consequence of the execution of the common criminal plan. And the Chamber even convicted four of them for foreseeing the risk that thefts were a probable consequence of the JCE's execution in Gornji Vakuf. In addition, each of the five are also convicted of thefts in at least one other municipality after Gornji Vakuf, and this pattern of thefts from Muslims, plunder and appropriation of property, continued through the execution of the common criminal plan. The Chamber's own findings are sufficient to fill the gaps that the Chamber left. Applying the correct legal and evidentiary standards, the findings that they've already made are sufficient to convict each of them for JCE 3 thefts. Since each of the respondents, each of the five respondents, already knew in January 1993 that thefts might occur in the execution of the joint criminal enterprise, then they could also foresee this risk in April in relation to Jablanica and May in Mostar and July in Stolac and Capljina and then in Prozor and Vares, especially since their knowledge of the violent discriminatory operations only grew over time and since they took no or at least no effective steps to stop the violence and property crimes. Your Honours, foreseeability does not depend on whether a particular respondent knew or did not know that a military attack was planned on a certain day in a certain place. Foreseeability does not require that kind of accurate prediction of the future. The Appeals Chamber already rejected that approach in the Krstic case. In response to a Defence complaint that he was being held responsible for crimes that he was unaware were actually occurring, the Appeals Chamber explained that for JCE 3 liability: "It is not necessary to establish that he was aware, in fact, that those other acts would have occurred." It was unnecessary for the Trial Chamber to determine whether the accused: "... was actually aware that those other criminal acts were being committed; it was sufficient that their occurrence was foreseeable to him and that those other crimes did in fact occur." And that's Krstic appeals judgement, paragraph 150. In a JCE of this nature and scale, it is legally sufficient for the type of crime to be foreseeable. And I would refer Your Honours to Sainovic appeals judgement, at paragraph 1089. Based on the nature of the JCE and the means used to implement it on the ground, the four types of JCE crimes were foreseeable to each of the respondents, and they were foreseeable regardless of whether a particular respondent knew about or was personally involved in the JCE 1 activities in that place on that day. And, Your Honours, the case law makes clear that it's not necessary for the purposes of JCE 3 responsibility that an accused be aware of the past occurrences of a crime for that type of crime to be foreseeable to him. Stanisic/Zupljanin paragraph 627. Actual notice of past crimes is not required. But each of the respondents in this case did in fact get such notice of past occurrences: Prlic as president, Stojic head of Department of Defence, Praljak and Petkovic at the top of the HVO's Main Staff, Coric as head of the military police administration, and Pusic in charge of prisoner releases and exchanges. From each of their positions and from their connections with each other and the other JCE members, each of them received information that serious crimes against people and property - going beyond even their intended crimes - were occurring in the course of their ethnic cleansing campaign. And this, Your Honours, is a good place to address question 4(c) from your order in relation to the Prosecution's appeal. If the Appeals Chamber were to reverse the Trial Chamber's conclusions concerning the murders at Sljivo's house and Dusa, would this have any impact on JCE liability? And the Prosecution's answer is: No, it would not. You've heard answers to this question from the Prosecution as respondent in relation to some of the Defence appeals last week; this connects with those submissions. Whether or not the killings of the seven civilians were found to qualify as murder and whether or not any of the respondents were privy to the contents of Siljeg's 28/29 January report, the fact remains that a clear pattern of attacks across Gornji Vakuf municipality on the 18th of January and over the following days followed a preconceived plan and unfolded in an atmosphere of extreme violence. And this climate of extreme violence continued throughout the implementation of the JCE, showing that this was the way that the common criminal purpose was intended to be implemented. In Sainovic, the Appeals Chamber considers that to foresee murder an accused must be aware not only of violence but of violence of such a level of gravity as to make the commission of murder foreseeable. What's different in this case, Your Honours, is that each of the JCE members was already found to have intended not only forcible displacement and persecution against Muslims, but also to murder Muslims as a JCE 1 crime. The Trial Chamber distinguished attack and forced labour murders as JCE 1 from eviction and detention murders as JCE 3, but it certainly bears on the foreseeability of the additional JCE 3 murders that murdering Muslims was already an intended means of achieving the common criminal purpose. So to sum up, by the time of the first JCE 3 murders, all of the respondents were aware of the extreme violence that was being used to achieve their common purpose, making murder a foreseeable JCE 3 crime, regardless of the legal classification of the Dusa killings or who received or was privy to the information contained in one of the reports about them. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's JCE 3 analysis is riddled with overlapping errors. The Chamber failed to properly adjudicate which of the respondents were criminally responsible for more than 70 per cent of the JCE 3 incidents; and for those incidents it did consider, it made factual and legal errors. We ask you to correct these errors and to convict the respondents as set out in our brief. Your Honours, I have a correction to transcript 14, line 5. I believe I misspoke. I said "after June 1993" the JCE members were found to have intended to spread terror and the other expanded crimes, and that should say "from June 1993." And that's volume 4, paragraph 59. Turning to ground 2 of the Prosecution's appeal. Again, this is the Chamber leaving the required analysis incomplete, entering an acquittal before all the charges in the indictment are adjudicated. The indictment charges each of the accused under Article 7(1) and Article 7(3). And when the Chamber acquitted under 7(1), its task was not yet finished; it still had to consider and adjudicate whether the defendants bore criminal responsibility as superiors. It did so with regard to the crimes in Prozor in 1992. Having found that there was no common criminal purpose at that point in time, it considered whether any of the defendants were nevertheless criminally responsible under alternative modes charged in the indictment. But for other crimes, when it found no criminal responsibility under JCE, it stopped prematurely. It entered an acquittal before addressing all of the charges in the indictment. We focussed on failure to punish because to be in this category of incompletely adjudicated crimes, the Trial Chamber has already made findings that there was no direct intent for JCE 1 and that the crimes were not foreseeable to that defendant for JCE 3. The only remaining mode of liability not excluded by that analysis would be Article 7(3), failure to punish. And we've set out in our brief the compelling facts and findings that should result in convictions for these crimes. To illustrate this error, let me take you to one example. The Chamber acquitted Petkovic for JCE 3 responsibility for the killing of four Muslim detainees at Dretelj prison in mid-July 1993; one died from dehydration and the other three were shot. The Chamber reasoned that Petkovic could not foresee these murders because he was only informed of them by the ICRC on 20 January 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: But before entering an acquittal, the Trial Chamber was required to look at the superior responsibility charges for this same incident. And this is not optional, it's not discretionary. Before entering an acquittal, the Trial Chamber has to adjudicate all of the modes charged in the indictment; and its own findings show that a conviction was warranted. The Trial Chamber found that Petkovic in the HVO Main Staff was the superior, he was the superior of and he had effective control over the perpetrators. Volume 4, paragraphs 663 and 679. And as I've just mentioned, the Trial Chamber found that he received -- that he was actually informed by the ICRC letter of these specific murders, albeit after they occurred. And the Chamber found that Petkovic accepted the mistreatment of detainees at Dretelj, including killings, and specifically that he failed to take any measures against the perpetrators. That's at paragraph 816. On the Chamber's own findings, all of the elements for superior responsibility failure to punish were established, yet no conviction for superior responsibility was entered. Instead, Petkovic has been acquitted of crimes even though the Chamber found that the elements of the crimes and the mode were proven. The Prosecution relies on the detailed arguments set out in our appeals brief. These erroneous acquittals should be reversed. Again, the Trial Chamber's primary responsibility is to fully adjudicate the indictment before it; and again, they've left justice left incomplete. And in ground 3, the Prosecution is again challenging a matter that is incomplete. It concerns a technical oversight in the Chamber's application of the cumulative convictions rule. When applying this rule, the Chamber erroneously allows four sets of incidents to fall out of the conviction. This error requires correction because the defendants were found to have committed crimes for which no convictions are then entered. Let me explain. The Chamber correctly found that the cumulative convictions rule prevented the Chamber from entering convictions based on the same facts for both the Article 2, grave breach of extensive destruction of property, which is charged as Count 19; and the Article 3 crime of wanton destruction, charged as Count 20. This is because only extensive destruction under Article 2 contains a distinct element, namely, that the property is generally protected under the Geneva Conventions or is located in occupied territory. All of the elements of the Article 3 wanton destruction are fully reflected in the Article 2 grave breach. Consequently, when the elements of both crimes are met based on the same facts, a conviction may only be entered for the extensive destruction under Article 2. And you can find that analysis at volume 4, paragraphs 1264 to 1266. The Chamber's analysis on this point is correct, and so far there is no dispute between the parties, no error in the trial judgement. The error occurs when the Trial Chamber applies the rule. In relation to four sets of incidents, the Chamber overlooks that it did not find criminal conduct under both Article 2 and Article 3. So in relation to these incidents, it overlooks that it doesn't really have a cumulative conviction situation in the first place. This ground affects only the destruction crimes in relation to Muslim homes in the four Gornji Vakuf villages on 18 January 1993, Muslim property in Prozor, ten mosques in East Mostar, and the destruction of the Old Bridge. Each of those four incidents was found to constitute the crime of wanton destruction, a violation of the laws and customs of war charged under Article 3 as Count 20. But for Count 19, the Chamber found that the elements were not met for each of these groups of incidents because the destruction did not occur on occupied territory and the property was not otherwise protected under the Geneva Conventions. Yet at the very end of judgement, the Chamber applies the cumulative conviction rule to the counts, the whole counts, as if there was perfect concurrence between the facts underlying the two crimes but there was not. So when the Chamber declined to enter a conviction for Count 20 based on the cumulative convictions rule, it drops these four incidents out of the convictions all together. You can find that at the disposition on pages 430 and 431 of volume 4. This was wrong. To correct this error, convictions under Count 20 should be reinstated for these four groups of incidents. And this is where I come to Your Honours' remaining question, question number 5, which relates to the Chamber's underlying legal findings about whether the attacks on the villages in Gornji Vakuf constituted wanton destruction or devastation not justified by military necessity. This is the Article 3 violation of the laws and customs of war charged as Count 20. This is the count for which the Trial Chamber did not enter a conviction because of its error in the application of the cumulative convictions rule. In the first part of the question, you've asked the Prosecution to discuss the basis for the Chamber's findings that the property destruction caused during the attacks on the villages of Dusa, Hrasnica, Zdrimci, and Uzricje was wanton and not justified by military necessity. Your Honours, in reaching its reasonable conclusion that the attacks were wanton, the Trial Chamber referred to the pattern across the four villages, noting that on 18 January 1993 the HVO damaged and destroyed many Muslim homes across the municipality. This was no coincidence. The attacks on the four villages were found by the Chamber to have unfolded in exactly the same way, beginning with the HVO first attacking the villages by firing shells at Muslim homes, then the HVO entered the villages, arrested the population, destroyed the remaining homes, and removed the villagers. Volume 4, paragraphs 561, 704, and 922. Based on this total similarity in the way that the operations unfolded and the crimes committed in each of the villages, the Chamber concluded that they corresponded to a preconceived plan. The Chamber found that the HVO attacked each of the four villages with mortar shells, heavy machine-guns, and artillery. Volume 2, paragraph 357. It characterised the shelling as indiscriminate. Volume 3, paragraph 711. As you heard last week, the HVO also used weapons to directly target Muslim civilian homes as happened in Dusa, where the HVO tank fired on and deliberately damaged Sljivo's house. The Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that the destruction of the homes lacked military justification. This was reasonable. None of the destroyed houses were military objects in and of themselves, and the Chamber took into consideration that there were a few ABiH members present in the villages at the times of the attacks. You can see the Chamber's analysis at volume 3, paragraph 1569; and volume 4, paragraph 45. And even that in one of the villages, Zdrimci, some armed Muslim men hid in houses from time to time. Again, volume 3, paragraph 1569; and volume 2, paragraph 382. But the existence of these village defenders, particularly in light of their small number and the fact that they were armed with hunting rifles and other small-arms, does not offer a plausible military justification for the selective destruction of Muslim property during these attacks. And the lack of military justification for the destructive attacks on civilian homes on the 18th of January is confirmed by the continuation of such destruction over the subsequent days, after the HVO had taken control of the four villages. The HVO removed the civilian population, it then systematically burned Muslim property that had not already been destroyed during the shelling operation, and the Trial Chamber found that this was done in order to prevent the Muslims from returning. Croat property was left intact. Volume 2, paragraph 414, 432, 456, and many others. In light of the totality of this evidence, the Chamber's finding that the destruction during the attack was wanton and not justified by military necessity is a reasonable one and should be upheld. In the second part of question 5, Your Honours, you've asked whether there would be any effect if this finding were overturned on the finding that the property destruction caused during the attacks on several localities in the municipalities was extensive. With regard to the trial judgement, the answer is no. There would be no effect on the Trial Judgement because, as I have just explained, as a result of the Chamber's cumulative conviction error, there is presently no conviction for the crime of extensive destruction on the 18th of January in the four villages. As found by the Chamber, the destruction in the days following the attacks would still meet the large-scale requirements for both Article 2 and Article 3 destruction crimes. But with regard to the Prosecution's appeal, the answer would be yes. If Your Honours found error in the Chamber's conclusion that the destruction was not justified by military necessity, then the only remaining destruction on 18th of January would be that in Gornji Vakuf town. And, Your Honours, the Prosecution has not appealed a cumulative conviction error in relation to Gornji Vakuf town. Your Honours, again in ground 3 the Prosecution's appeal is focussed on an incomplete adjudication. The Trial Chamber concluded that each of the respondents were guilty but then failed to enter a conviction. In this third way, justice has been left incomplete. And with that, Your Honours, I'd conclude my submissions and hand the podium over to my colleague, Ms. Goy, to discuss sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. By sentencing the respondents to between 10 and 25 years of imprisonment, the Chamber abused its discretion. These sentences are manifestly inadequate. The respondents are convicted for having implemented a protracted campaign of ethnic cleansing to create Croat domination in Herceg-Bosna. The crimes occurred throughout a large part of BiH, covering eight municipalities. The crimes were massive in scale. Tens of thousands of Muslims were evicted from their homes, often expelled across the border through an elaborate system, thousands were arrested and detained in awful conditions, many were forced to perform dangerous labour on the front line. Muslims were killed during attacks or when forced to work on the front line. They were raped, they were sexually assaulted. Muslim houses and mosques were destroyed, Muslim property plundered. Over 50.000 people were trapped in East Mostar by late August 1993. They were subjected to relentless shelling and sniping. The respondents played key roles in the joint criminal enterprise to create Croat domination by criminal means. They were the JCE's architects and their leading implementers. In light of the gravity of the crimes themselves and the key roles the respondents played in them, their sentences of 10 to 25 years are so unreasonable that they constitute an abuse of discretion. In today's hearing, I would invite Your Honours to look at the Chamber's sentencing analysis from two different perspectives. Both perspectives show that the sentences imposed are too low and constitute an abuse of discretion. First, I propose to look at the Chamber's own conclusions on the gravity, the gravity of the crimes themselves and the roles of the accused. We will see that the Chamber's conclusions are not in line with the sentences it imposed; this shows that the Chamber failed to give gravity adequate weight. Second, I propose to look at a number of specific features of this case, features which confirm that the sentences imposed are manifestly inadequate. Starting with my first point. The sentences of 25 years for Prlic, 20 years for Stojic, Praljak and Petkovic, 16 years for Coric and, 10 years for Pusic are manifestly unreasonable when one looks at the Chamber's own conclusions in the sentencing part of the judgement. And here we recognise that sentencing is a matter of discretion, but this discretion has to be exercised in a way that gives adequate weight to the gravity of the crimes themselves and the form and degree of participation within the available sentencing range. And the available sentencing range is up to life imprisonment. The highest fixed-term sentences imposed at the ICTY and the ICTR are in the 40s, with 40 years' imprisonment imposed against Milomir Stakic and 47 years' imprisonment imposed by the Appeals Chamber for two accused in the Butare case. So this is the sentencing framework in which the Chamber has to exercise its discretion. With this framework in mind, I would invite Your Honours now to look with me at three aspects of the Chamber's gravity analysis: One, the Chamber's conclusion on the gravity of the crimes themselves; two, the Chamber's conclusion on the form of responsibility; and three, the Chamber's conclusion on the degree of participation. Starting with the Chamber's findings on the gravity of the crimes. The Trial Chamber concluded that the crimes of which the respondents were found guilty were extremely serious. It said: "The scale and brutality of the crimes, on the one hand, and the inherent nature of the offences, on the other, show that the crimes committed by the accused are extremely serious." Volume 4, paragraph 1302. It is clear from the rest of the judgement that this conclusion is an appropriate characterisation of the crimes committed by the respondents. These crimes included the eviction of tens of thousands, killings during attack and while performing dangerous forced labour on the front line, the detention in terrible conditions, the daily shelling and shooting in the small area of East Mostar where more than 50.000 people were trapped from late August 1993. Next, I would invite Your Honours to look at the Chamber's findings on the form of responsibility. The Chamber found all respondents criminally liable as members of a joint criminal enterprise. Joint criminal enterprise liability is considered one of the most serious forms of responsibility. That's the Mrksic appeals judgement, paragraph 407; and Krnojelac appeals judgement, paragraph 75. Turning now to the Chamber's findings on the degree of participation. The Chamber found all respondents played a key role, in the French original "un rôle majeur", in the commission of the crimes. Volume 4, paragraphs 1317, 1318 for Prlic; 1329, 1330 for Stojic; 1341, 1342 for Praljak; and 1354, 1355 for Petkovic; 1369, 1370 for Coric; and 1381 for Pusic. Four of them, Prlic, Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic, were even found to be key members of the JCE. In the French original, "des membres les plus importants." Volume 4, paragraphs 1315, 1328, 1340, and 1353. To sum up, the Chamber found the crimes were extremely serious; it found all respondents guilty under one of the most serious forms of responsibility, joint criminal enterprise; and it found that Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak were one of the most important members of the JCE and that all of the respondents, including Coric and Pusic, played a major role in the commission of the crimes. On the basis of these conclusions, one would reasonably have expected sentences in the high range of fixed-term sentences for Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak, and at least in the upper part for Coric and Pusic. This raises the question: Is there another explanation for the far lower sentences imposed or can they only be explained by an abuse of discretion? Can the mitigating factors explain the reduction that must have occurred had the Chamber given gravity and the form and degree of participation adequate weight? The answer is no. As mitigating factors, the Chamber found for all respondents voluntary surrender and good behaviour in detention and on provisional release. Voluntary surrender and good behaviour in detention may warrant some mitigation, as the Kordic appeal judgement found paragraph 1053. But they cannot explain the major reduction that must have occurred had the Chamber given gravity and the form and degree of participation adequate weight. In particular, as the Appeals Chamber found in Krajisnik, good conduct in detention could only have a limited impact on the sentences in light of the gravities of the crimes. That's the Krajisnik appeals judgement in paragraphs 816, 817. And in any event, in addition to the mitigating factors, the Chamber also had to take into account the aggravating factor of abuse of authority in relation to all respondents. For Prlic and Petkovic, the Chamber took additional mitigating factors into account. For Prlic, the Trial Chamber also considered his post-conflict conduct in mitigation; however, in light of the aggravating factor, this cannot reduce a sentence in the high range of fixed-term sentences to 25 years' imprisonment. For Petkovic the Chamber found two other mitigating factors: Absence of criminal records and preference for negotiations. But the Chamber determined itself that both had limited weight, in light of the gravity of the crimes and the scope of Petkovic's participation and his efforts to conceal HVO responsibility. Volume 4, paragraphs 1359, 1361. Thus, here as well the mitigating factors cannot explain the reduction from what one could reasonably have expected to be a sentence in the high range of fixed-term sentences to 20 years' imprisonment. To conclude the first part of my submissions, the Chamber found that the crimes were extremely serious, the respondents were responsible under one of the most serious forms of responsibility, and they played key roles in the commission of the crime. Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak were even found to be most important members of the JCE. In light of these findings, the Chamber's sentences imposed are manifestly inadequate. These sentences cannot be explained by the mitigating factors found. The sentences imposed can simply not be squared with the Chamber's own conclusions. The Chamber 's own conclusions are rather in line with the sentences requested by the Prosecution, both at trial and now on appeal: 40 years for Prlic, Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic; 35 years for Coric; and 25 years for Pusic. The only explanation for the far lower sentences imposed is that the Chamber did not give adequate weight to the gravity of the crimes themselves and the form and degree of participation. The only explanation available is that the Chamber abused its discretion. Let me now turn to the second part of my argument. The Chamber's abuse of discretion becomes not only obvious when one compares its conclusion on the gravity with the sentences imposed. That the sentences are manifestly inadequate is also obvious when one looks at the features of the case, features that makes the crimes particularly grave. I will address four of these features: The scale of the crimes; the vicious siege of East Mostar; the system of expulsion through a network of detention facilities; and the use of unlawful, dangerous forced labour. First of all, the crimes were of a large scale. Tens of thousands of Muslims were displaced, thousands were arrested and detained in terrible conditions, mistreated, or killed; over 50.000 were subjected to unlawful attack and terror in East Mostar. Second, the vicious siege of East Mostar is another feature of this case which made the crimes particularly grave. To avoid any misunderstanding, Your Honour, the Prosecution is not arguing that the Trial Chamber overlooked the siege, but rather, that the Chamber failed to analyse its inherent gravity and to give it sufficient weight. Two aspects indicate that the Chamber failed to give the siege sufficient weight: The cursory way the Chamber dealt with the siege in the sentencing part of the judgement and a comparison with sentences imposed in other cases involving a siege. The Chamber failed to sufficiently analyse the inherent gravity of the siege. For ten months the HVO besieged east Mostar. The HVO subjected the besieged population to relentless shelling and sniping. Over 50.000 people were trapped in overcrowded East Mostar by late August 1993. The HVO's shelling and sniping during the siege killed or injured hundreds and caused substantial damage to homes, mosques, the Old Bridge, and the only hospital. The population of East Mostar, including women, children, and elderly, lived under the constant shelling and gun-fire, under the constant threat of being hit, wounded, or killed. They were terrified. The HVO made the situation even worse by blocking or hindering humanitarian aid. The brutality of the siege is clearly shown by the BBC documentary by Jeremy Bowen, who was present in East Mostar in August and September 1993, during a time when all respondents were JCE members. That is Exhibit P06365. Bowen said that Mostar was the most devastated city, worse than Sarajevo and Vukovar. That's at 34.56, through 35.05. I would invite Your Honours now to watch three clips of the video which show the conditions in besieged East Mostar. And for the record, these are at 1.25 through 4.05; 11.20 to 12.27; and 16.36 to 17.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: "There are no safe places in East Mostar. You can be killed or maimed at any time on any street corner. Until you see it happening, it's hard to realise how quickly lives can be destroyed. Franjo Pavlovic, who was born a Croat, made the mistake of going out to repair some shell damage on what had started out as quiet morning. Because Raima, his wife, is a Muslim, the Croats expelled them over the front line into East Mostar in August. He had one chance, a fire engine, the only one left on this side of Mostar, was nearby. Perhaps it could get him to the hospital in time. Nothing in her life before the war had prepared Mrs. Pavlovic for this. She's 53. After they married, she worked as an accountant in a graphic design business. The last traces of that life disappeared when her husband was hit. The streets were empty and not just because of the shelling. There is a six-hour-long day-time curfew; the idea is to stop people getting hurt. The hospital was only a few minutes away. Nothing is more than a few minutes away in East Mostar. "The doctor hardly had to look at him. Mr. Pavlovic was dead. He had been killed by shrapnel in the chest. For her sake he went through the motions. "'You haven't examined him yet,' she said. 'Please do more.' "Everything from the explosion to this had taken about ten minutes. The hospital was ready for the next casualties."

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: "Refugees started appearing in no man's land. ... "He told them to hurry and to take cover. Often the Croats start shooting once they've forced Muslims out of West Mostar through this section of the front line. Fatima and Salin Matic had just been thrown out of their home by Croat gunmen. Mr. Matic, who is 72, managed to put on three shirts and to grab two umbrellas as he left. "His wife, who Is 70, was still in her nightclothes. Their neighbour, 84-year-old Mrs. Almassa Humo, arrived a few minutes later. 'Don't sit there,' they told her, 'they could kill you.' "Even if Mrs. Humo still cared, she didn't have the strength to move any further on her own."

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: "The civilians know that their only hope is to help themselves, to hang on until the killing ends, to survive the winter. But how do you avoid pneumonia, bronchitis and worse when shells have smashed your roof. These people are refugees. They live in a ruin, like thousands of others in East Mostar. "She can't walk. She lies in stinking clothes on a soaking bed. "'What can I do? Either I die or go on living like this.'"

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: With the siege of East Mostar, the implementation of the JCE took up a new dimension. The JCE members added unlawful attacks on civilians, terror and destruction of religious property to the criminal means used to achieve their purpose. The sentences imposed show that the Chamber did not give this vicious siege sufficient weight. Another indication that the Chamber did not give the relentless shelling and sniping during the siege sufficient weight is a comparison with the sentences imposed in the cases against Stanislav Galic and Dragomir Milosevic. They were sentenced to life imprisonment and 29 years' imprisonment respectively for a shelling and sniping campaign during the siege in Sarajevo. And here we recognise that the cases of Galic and Dragomir Milosevic are not identical to the ones of the respondents in this case. But the unlawful attack on civilians and terror during the siege in both Sarajevo and Mostar show enough similarities to make a comparison meaningful. Galic and Dragomir Milosevic were sentenced to life imprisonment and 29 years respectively for crimes committed during the siege of Sarajevo, including unlawful attacks and terror. In this case, the crimes for which the respondents were convicted include unlawful attacks and terror during the siege of Mostar, but the crime base is much broader. It includes unlawful and dangerous forced labour, even murder during forced labour and during attacks on towns and villages; it includes unlawful imprisonment and detention in terrible conditions; and it includes the expulsion of tens of thousands. The comparison of the sentences imposed in this case with the sentences of life imprisonment and 29 years in Galic and Dragomir Milosevic show that the sentences imposed by this Chamber are unreasonable. This brings me to the third feature I would like to address: The highly organised system of expelling Muslims from Croat-claimed areas and BiH altogether. In this case, the displacement was brought to near perfection through the use of a highly organised and effective system of expulsion involving a network of detention facilities. The JCE members arrested and detained thousands of Muslims. They were detained in harsh conditions, where they were mistreated beaten and abused. To escape the horrible conditions, the detainees had to agree to leave Herceg-Bosna and BiH - often with their families - once released. The releases were thus made contingent upon the Muslims leaving from Croat-claimed territories. The network of detention facilities was a key aspect of the joint criminal enterprise. It spanned across the Croat-claimed territories. It included the Heliodrom in Mostar, Dretelj, and Gabela prisons in Capljina; the Vitina Otok camp; the Vojno detention centre; Ljubuski prison; and numerous others which the Chamber listed in footnote 1677 of volume 4. This system of expulsion through the network of detention facilities was introduced at least by the end of June 1993, when all respondents were JCE members; through it, the implementation of the JCE became more efficient. Volume 4, paragraph 64. For example, in Stolac, none of the 8.000 Muslims remained. The sentences imposed suggest that the Chamber did not give this sinister system adequate weight. The fourth feature that makes the crimes of this case particularly grave is the widespread use of detainees for dangerous, unlawful forced labour at the front line. The JCE members forced prisoners of war as well as civilians, including at a very young age to perform dangerous labour. One victim was just 13 years old. Volume 3, paragraph 1510. For ten months between May 1993 and March 1994, the JCE members forced detainees to build or repair military fortifications or shelters, dig trenches, lug heavy cases of ammunition, or collect and bury bodies of soldiers. Volume 3, paragraph 1514; volume 4, paragraph 1167. The victims had to carry out forced labour under dangerous conditions, some were wounded, others even killed. This was part of the JCE members' plan, and all respondents played key roles in the implementation of this plan for various periods of time. The Chamber failed to give this widespread use of forced labour adequate weight. To conclude, Your Honours, four specific features highlight the extreme seriousness of the crimes for which the respondents were convicted: Their large scale; the vicious siege of East Mostar; the highly organised system of expulsions; and the widespread and dangerous use of detainees for unlawful forced labour. All respondents implemented the plan in which these criminal means were used to achieve Croat domination in Herceg-Bosna. All respondents played key roles in its implementation. The sentences imposed show that the Chamber cannot have given the gravity of the crimes or the form and degree of participation adequate weight. Had the Chamber given these factors adequate weight, it would have imposed sentences of between 25 and 40 years of imprisonment, 40 years for Prlic, Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic, 35 for Coric, and 25 years for Pusic. Such sentences would have been in line with the Chamber's own conclusions on the gravity of the crime and the form and degree of participation of the respondents. Thank you, Your Honours. Unless you have any questions, this ends the Prosecution's main submissions.

utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prlic, and this is our final direction to you. The Prosecution appeal is mainly -- not mainly, almost completely on JCE 3 and then a question on sentencing, and you can only address those two issues today. Anything else I will stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Okay, I have to leave at that. [Interpretation] Why was JCE applied as a type of liability with a single criminal intent? That remains to be a key issue in this courtroom. In our appeal we did not object to the jurisprudence of the joint criminal enterprise, although that could be discussed at length, but the way in which it was applied. Because even the most liberally applied variant could not be supported by the facts in this case. The JCE cannot be derived only from a political intention or even a military order that my colleague Ms. Nozica discussed. We have seen on last Thursday that there is -- all the orders of the Main Staff. There is no order for attack by the HVO in the entire period. Even an order to attack would not mean anything because - according to this logic - every military operation would mean culpability by the person who ordered it. There must be a criminal intent, which of course can be established based on circumstance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, I stop you. And, in any case, what you are saying is not going to be taken into account because this is not about JCE 3.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: I'm approaching to JCE 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, go to JCE 3. You're -- this is not an interesting, touristic adventure. Go straight to JCE 3 and to sentencing, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] [In English] ... to sentence before JCE 3. [Interpretation] The criminal enterprise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't let you have it your way, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay, apologise -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's us five up here --

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- who conduct the orchestra. Okay? You do as we say; otherwise, I will ask you to sit down and that will be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] Under circumstances when the criminal enterprise is construed only based on a political idea, how can we discuss JCE 3 when even the important elements of JCE 1 are not met? We are coming close to the -- to a dangerous precedent, namely, accusing of crime anyone, a president, a commander at any level, even of the smallest unit, simply for sending soldiers to war, even if that commander, like me, was never in the chain of command. Judgement volume 4, paragraph 106. And the political idea on which the criminal intent is based is the alleged Tudjman's obsession with Banovina. And whatever is said or done, it's immediately dismissed as a double or duplicitous policy. Even the noblest act as the unparalleled support of Croatia and Croats to the BH and Muslims was, with the basic aim to reject any federalisation of the country, which was a constant of all international plans. For those who want to see the consistently of Tudjman's position that I discussed on day one, here is what he said in his intimate circle between 1992 and 1994 on different topics important to this case which are contrary to the taken out of context citations that served as a basis for establishing the alleged criminal intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, I have to stop you again. Mr. Prlic, this -- it's perhaps due to your complete lack of knowledge about law and procedure, but although you purported to mention and go straight to JCE 3, we are being given a lesson in history. I'm not interested in that. I'm only interested in the elements of JCE 3 as they have been suggested by the Prosecution and what's your defence for that. The rest you can take back home with you.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: I just want to say there is no JCE 3 without JCE 1 and if JCE 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could have said that already.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: It is not resumed yet. I had to strengthen my case. There is no JCE 3. This is direct answer on today discussion by OTP. If it is possible to use my time, I will appreciate; if it is not possible, I'm going to sit down and that's it. I think it is important if you want to have all elements to be able to make your decision. I just tried to help Bench, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're certainly not helping yourself, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have taken my risk by intending to say what I want to say. I'm fully aware of that, and this 20 minutes doesn't mean anything. But if you decide another way, I have no other possibility than to accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, let's...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, the President has been trying to help you and he has suggested that you would have been much better served in your interests had you asked you lawyer to speak for you.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You still have a few minutes left and if I were you I would give five minutes or so to your lawyer to present your case, because you are not doing any good to yourself --

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- Mr. President has pointed out.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, don't tell me have you not prepared yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, 35 years of practicing law I have never come to court unprepared. I am prepared. May I ask how much time do we have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have 12 or 13 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Since I won't be able to use all my 13 minutes before we take a break, could we take a break now -- it doesn't matter to me. I can go now and go through the 13 minutes or take a break and -- whichever you wish, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will be very brief. The Prosecution today said a couple of interesting things. First, they said that the scale of omissions was unparalleled -- I think it was unprecedented and unacceptable. They also said the Trial Chamber is responsible to fully adjudicate the indictment. I could not agree more. But are they not also responsible for assessing all of the evidence? Are they also not responsible to issue reasoned decisions? Now if you go through their brief, because -- and they mentioned this throughout today's presentation, you will see that they occasionally say the Chamber unduly limited the scope of the evidence it deemed relevant, it erred by compartmentalising and analysing the evidence, that the Chamber analysed the evidence in isolation, that the Chamber must consider all evidence presented to it and assess and weigh the evidence in its totality and in context. This is in their brief and this is what they were saying today, that for some reason - for some reason - when the Trial Chamber came to this part of the judgement they sort of stopped. The implication being with everything else they were doing a great job, but with this part they just simply failed to analyse properly, they compartmentalised. They didn't take into account all of the evidence, they failed to consider its own findings and relevant evidence that provided context to the incidents, they limited their consideration of evidence, and so on. And I ask: Is that not what we have been saying all along? And is that not what we believe runs throughout - permeates throughout - this entire judgement? The Prosecution says today: Well, Dr. Jadranko Prlic and the others committed all these other crimes, they were foreseeable, and the Trial Chamber simply failed to look at all of the evidence. For somehow they were compartmentalising. They didn't do their job. They didn't properly assess. We submit, Your Honours, that that has merit, their argument has merit, as our argument that in looking at all of the evidence, the Trial Chamber failed or cherry-picked what it believed, you know, was relevant to their version of the events, to where they wanted to go. So we don't accept the idea that somehow the Trial Chamber failed to make a proper assessment with respect to JCE 3. I think they were at a loss because there was a lot of evidence. They were at a loss because the Prosecution had an overly broad indictment where they tried to charge anything and everything for everything to the accused as if they're omnipresent and omnipotent. If you look at our submissions concerning the sentencing, Your Honours, and I believe they're in - one moment - they're in paragraphs 185 to 248 of our response. We deal with the issue of the sentence, because they say the sentence was relatively low in comparison to the gravity of the events and what have you. We don't minimise the human tragedy in this case. We don't minimise the fact that there was a lot of destruction, loss of human life, inhumane treatment. But if you look at those paragraphs, in those paragraphs of our response, we go chapter and verse through the responsibilities and the powers of Dr. Prlic. We tried to explain to the Appeals Chamber how the HZ HB functioned, what were its responsibilities, why it was created, and what it was intending to do. It doesn't mean that crimes were not committed, but the whole purpose of a trial is to determine who is responsible for the crimes, not who is available to be tried. We submit, Your Honour, that throughout this trial, the Trial Chamber erred -as the Prosecution has said not just for their part but for the entire trial, the entire judgement - they failed to assess the evidence properly. And we submit that as a matter of due process, equality of arms -- because we believe equality of arms extends not just to the resources but also to the manner in which the case is tried and the evidence is assessed. They come here today and they say: Give us justice because the Trial Chamber did not assess the evidence properly; we say the same. We say look at the evidence critically. Look at what we've cited. They continually use the Mladic diaries. They use it in -- they didn't say it today but they used it in their response. We say look at chapter -- look at ground 5 of our appeal, look at ground 5 of our reply. And therein you will see that the Trial Chamber - despite Judge Antonetti's reasoned opinion or reasoned decision or his analysis - that 38 out of 40 excerpts of the Mladic diaries should be assessed, this is what we submitted, 38 out of 40. It wasn't the Trial Chamber, as my good friend Mr. Stringer said, but it was the minority -- the majority that said no, they cannot come in. The Prosecution comes in today and say: The Trial Chamber looked at things out of context with respect to JCE 3. We say they looked out of context with regard to JCE 1 and with respect to the entire Defence case. And so what's good for the goose is good for the gander. We say: Look at everything, not just some of it. I don't want to take up your time because you have the briefs. The briefs, in my humble submission, are very well written. They are very well -- we cite all the relevant authority. And we present everything that we think is necessary for your consideration. The Defence -- the Prosecution says: Well, for some reason, the Trial Chamber failed. We submit for some reason the majority, in particular, failed because they approached this case with a determination -- with a destination in mind, and here is where I want to end. If I could have the one slide, Suzana, up. The two slides I want to say, because I don't want to give the impression that I'm suggesting that the Judges were unfair, but I do make the suggestion - as I believe Mr. Khan did - that at some point the Judges, especially the majority, might have been looking at the evidence from a particular perspective because after all you will see -- this is on the web site. If I could look at the other one. This is on the official web site of the ICTY and this was on the web site or flyers to this effect were already in existence prior to the judgement. The republic's strategic position made it subject to both Serbia and Croatia attempting to assert dominance --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Pardon me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- over large chunks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you appear to be going again into your grounds of appeal. Your Honours, we have an objection again on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecution was the one that was -- been complaining all morning that for some reason when it came to their evidence on JCE 3, they totally ignored and compartmentalised. I'm entitled to show that they did the same thing with us, and this is a good example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and I know it may be embarrassing for the Court to be looking at this, but we suggest that when it came to assessing the evidence for the Defence, whether it was regard to JCE 3 or otherwise, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two wrongs do not make a right. You have already made your point as to how you were treated by the first Court, by the Trial Chamber. You had -- you had a good two hours, one of which was stolen away from you by your client. But what we expect from you today is to tell us whether Ms. Baig and her colleague are correct in their submission or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I find it hard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you tell us: We were treated like that as well, you are indirectly telling us that they were right, they were ignored by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I find it hard to believe, Your Honour, that the Prosecution would have the temerity to suggest that the Trial Chamber was only unfair to them and not unfair to the Defence. Is it possible -- is it credible to suggest that only when it came to certain counts of the JCE 3, the Trial Chamber adopted this compartmentalisation process, they decided not to assess the evidence properly, they did not look at everything that was available? We suggest that that is not the case, but we do suggest that throughout the trial that is what happened to all of the accused; and that's why we ended up with the result that we ended. What Dr. Prlic was trying to say is with respect to JCE 3 that was mentioned today, that if you look at his role and his responsibilities and his functions and if you look at all of the facts that were presented, you will see that you don't get to JCE 1; and if you can't get to JCE 1, you can't get to JCE 3. So for us at this stage to try to counter the points on JCE 3 that they're making today, we find somewhat ludicrous, if you will, because we do not accept the notion that Dr. Prlic was engaged in a joint criminal enterprise and was involved in any capacity to any of those events and is not responsible for any of the events. And therefore, it is difficult to go and argue point by point on whether the Trial Chamber should or should not have found Dr. Jadranko Prlic guilty of JCE 3 with respect to certain events. You have to look at his responsibilities and you have to look at the Trial Chamber's analysis of the facts and their conclusions that there was this overarching JCE, which is why I believe my client was trying to address some of the issues with respect to Tudjman. We appreciate the time that you have given to us to make our submissions, we apologise for any inconvenience, and we are certainly grateful to your patience today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have half an hour -- actually, we will start at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Defence for Mr. Stojic. You have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Our reply to the appeal by the Prosecution and we have with us our consultant Aidan Ellis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELLIS
utterances.text: In response to the Prosecution appeal, we don't assert that this trial judgement is perfect. How could we, Your Honours, when we've asserted so many errors in it ourselves? Your Honours will have noted already from our response brief that where points are clear that there are errors, we've tried to concede the points. For example, in paragraphs 145 or 146 of our response brief. But despite those errors, Your Honours, we say that the Prosecution failed to eliminate any reasonable doubt of Stojic's guilt in relation to grounds 1, 2, and aspects of ground 3; and further, that they failed to show that the 20-year sentence imposed on Stojic is unjust and plainly unreasonable. We propose to focus today on grounds 1 and ground 4, as the Prosecution did. For the detail, of course, we stand by every point in our written submissions. And, Your Honours, in those written submissions we deal with each head of the Prosecution's ground 1 in relation to JCE 3. But the overarching reason why all of those heads of ground 1 should be dismissed is a simple one. When the correct legal standard is applied to the Trial Chamber's findings, the Prosecution has failed to eliminate reasonable doubt that the deviatory crimes were foreseeable to Stojic. And therefore, the Trial Chamber did not err in entering acquittals and no new convictions should be entered. Your Honours, I'll deal with the law briefly because it seems there's no real distance between the Prosecution and the Defence on the key issue. The Prosecution submit that the Trial Chamber erred by applying a probability standard rather than a possibility standard, and it's right that the test defined by the Appeals Chamber is not one of probability; although we do say it's not quite accurately described as a test of mere probability either. It's important in our submission to preserve a meaningful test of foreseeability, and the reason why it's important is that convicting the accused pursuant to JCE 3 means convicting them of crimes that they did not intend and which fell outside the scope of the common purpose. That's why a meaningful foreseeability threshold is required, otherwise the result is the involvement in a common criminal purpose could lead to an open-ended liability for crimes committed thereafter. And we say the test defined in the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence is a meaningful threshold. The Prosecution cited this morning to Sainovic, to paragraph 18 of the Karadzic JCE 3 foreseeability decision. And the tests cited in those cases isn't one of mere possibility; it's whether the possibility that the crime could be committed is sufficiently substantial as to be foreseeable to the accused, the accused as an individual. That nuance, that subtlety in the reasoning isn't caught by just describing this as a possibility test. There is a spectrum of likelihood. On that spectrum, the test isn't as high as probability, but it's not as low as mere possibility either and it's not caught by implausibility remote scenarios. We would highlight from the many detailed submissions in our brief two points today. First, that considering relevant location-specific factors should lead the Appeals Chamber to dismiss all aspects of ground 1; and second, that the documents relied on by the Prosecution are insufficient in any event to eliminate doubt as to Stojic's guilt. For clarity, when I refer to "incidents," Your Honours, I'm using the language and the numbering used by the Prosecution at tables 53 -- the table on page 53 to 57 of their appeal brief.
