And to deal first with location-specific factors. We say they are important in this case because of the scale of the crime base considered in the indictment. Where there are so many different locations and where crimes are committed over a period of so many month, we say that what is foreseeable to one accused in one location at one time is not necessarily foreseeable to them many months later, in a distant location. And it appears again there's a measure of agreement between the parties here. Paragraph 12 of the Prosecution consolidated reply at least accepts that location-specific factors are not irrelevant. And what's important about them is not to suggest that Stojic must make a contribution to the crimes in each municipality. We know that's not the point. The point about location-specific factors is that they identify the knowledge that the accused have, knowledge of particular vulnerabilities of civilian populations, knowledge of particular propensities of particular units. And the problem, we say, with this judgement in relation to JCE 3 is that there are very limited factual findings about Stojic's knowledge in many of the locations for which the Prosecution invite Your Honours to enter new convictions. Take the example of Stolac, with an apology if my pronunciation is wrong Your Honours. There the Prosecution invites to you enter JCE 3 convictions for two incidents of murder, one appropriation of property. That's incidents 5, 6, and 26. What findings then did the Trial Chamber make about Stojic's role in crimes in that municipality or his personal knowledge of operations there? None, we say, none whatsoever. And in those circumstances, we say it's untenable to enter new convictions in relation to that municipality. And there are many other examples, Your Honours. In Prozor municipality, where the Prosecution invite you to enter six new convictions, incidents 1, 14 through 16, 21, and 24. In the section of the judgement addressing Stojic's responsibility municipality by municipality, it's only paragraph 329 of volume 4 that has anything to say about Prozor. And Your Honours will recall that factual finding from the very final slide that we displayed in the course of our reply submissions on Tuesday. It's the occasion when a particular report, P3418, was found to have been received by two of the defendants but the Trial Chamber managed to reach opposite findings in respect of their knowledge on the basis of that document. Contrast paragraph 329 and paragraph 799 of volume 4. Apart from that unreasonable finding, no other findings about Stojic's knowledge or the circumstances in Prozor at the time when the deviatory crimes occur. Very limited factual findings also in relation to Vares, where taking volume 4, paragraph 380 at its highest - and of course Stojic has appealed those findings - but taken at their highest, his involvement comes days after the crimes were committed. And here is where we really part company with the Prosecution because it's said today that Your Honours can safely enter new convictions on the new JCE counts without requiring extensive appellate fact-finding, that you can move straight from the general findings about contextual factors to enter convictions against Stojic. We say that's wrong, Your Honours. We say that that would require Your Honours at least to consider the factual position in relation to knowledge of circumstances in each of the municipalities concerned. And on that, the Trial Chamber's judgement simply does not assist, Your Honours. It doesn't leave behind the necessary building blocks, the factual foundations and findings, on which Your Honours could build new convictions. And we would say that reflects limited factual evidence in the record about Stojic's knowledge of circumstances in those municipalities. Absent those location-specific factors, the Prosecution cannot establish beyond reasonable doubt that deviatory crimes were foreseeable to Stojic, and that should be fatal to ground 1 of the appeal on its own. But in any event, Your Honours, my second point. The documents and findings relied on are not sufficient to establish that the deviatory crimes, that the possibility that they might occur, were sufficiently substantial as to be foreseeable to Stojic. There is one error that we say crops up throughout the Prosecution's submissions, and it's the repeated reliance on documents that were simply sent to the Defence Department generally as evidence that proves beyond reasonable doubt that Stojic knew about the content of those documents. That does not necessarily follow, Your Honours. The Department of Defence was not an insubstantial administrative body. The Trial Chamber found that it had six sectors: Main Staff, civil protection, security, health, ethics and morals, and procurement. It was administered through various offices, and each of those sectors was headed by an assistant chief with their own responsibilities for the work of that sector. This is from volume 1, paragraph 540. And, Your Honour, there was evidence about what was supposed to happen when a document was actually received by the Defence Department. There was evidence that the Defence Department stamped documents on receipt. That's not surprising. Most administrative bodies do something similar, but it appears in the transcript at 36247, lines 3 to 21. Your Honours, I will admit that on occasion I struggled with the different stamps applied to the original documents in this case, but I commend P1880 to Your Honours as an example of a document bearing the stamp to show it was received by the Defence Department. And Your Honours will see that the stamp simply says "Defence Department Mostar." Nothing else on it to indicate, for example, that it's gone to a different branch, like the SIS, as we see on some documents. But in relation to many of the documents that the Prosecution relies on, there's no evidence or finding that they were actually seen by Stojic. Take paragraph 24 of the Prosecution reply which introduces P1915 as evidence that the Defence Department were informed of the preparations for operations in Jablanica in April 1993. No stamp on that document to indicate it was received by the Defence Department. The stamp on the original that Your Honours will see relates to the Main Staff; that's presumably why the Trial Chamber specifically found it was received by the Main Staff. Volume 4, paragraph 714. But no equivalent finding that the Defence Department saw it. In fact, the Trial Chamber established - it's volume 4, paragraph 441 - that Stojic was informed of HVO operations in Jablanica after they had taken place, which is obviously inconsistent with the reliance now placed on P1915. And there are many other documents cited in the appeal brief and the reply brief of the Prosecution, where the same comments would apply. P4161, P648, P4177, and P2063, to give only four examples, not addressed to Stojic personally, not bearing Stojic's Department of Defence stamp, and no other way to establish beyond doubt that they were received by him. No witness to testify that they passed the document to him. The Defence tried to assist the Tribunal by locating the Defence Department register, which would have conclusively listed all of these documents that were received by that department; but unfortunately the register could not be found. See 2D1399 for our efforts to find that document. Your Honour, the result of the absence of that document is that there is doubt that Stojic ever personally saw many of the documents relied on throughout the Prosecution appeal brief. For reasons of time, I'll move swiftly through this, Your Honours, but we also assert in our response brief that a number of the documents that the Prosecution rely on turn out to be dated after a number of the incidents on which they seek convictions. In relation to murder or wilful killing in detention, amongst the documents cited by the Prosecution at P4352 and P4161, both dated August 1993. But the Prosecution is inviting Your Honours to enter convictions for killings in detentions that begin with incident 2 in April 1993, four months earlier. In fact, only part of one incident was committed after the date of P4352. So the submission on this part of ground 1 comes down to this. In relation to each of the deviatory crimes the Prosecution rely on a small number of documents to try to prove that Stojic was on notice that those crimes might occur. But once Your Honours exclude those documents that post-date the incidents, once you exclude those documents which it cannot be established that Stojic saw, once -- we hope Your Honours will also exclude the evidence in relation to P1351 and Gornji Vakuf for the reasons given last week. We say what remains is wholly insufficient to eliminate reasonable doubt that the deviatory crimes were foreseeable to Stojic. And so ground 1 of the Prosecution appeal should be dismissed. Your Honours, I move now to ground 4, sentence. At the start of this appeal hearing, Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, remind the parties that these appeals are not a trial de novo, that the parties must refrain from repeating their cases which were presented at trial, but the Prosecution appeal against sentence is exactly that; it's a repetition of their case which was presented at trial. The Prosecution continues its pursuit of a 40-year sentence for Stojic, exactly the sentence it sought at trial. And as we've pointed out in paragraph 182 of our response brief, many of the Prosecution's written submissions - indeed many of the oral submissions today - bear more than a passing resemblance to the final trial brief or the closing trial arguments. We say the Prosecution failed to identify error in the Chamber's approach to sentencing, that the Trial Chamber didn't impose the sentence that they asked for does not establish error. Your Honours, we say the test was set down for similar Prosecution appeal against sentence in Galic, with the majority concluding at paragraphs 455 and 456 that the Appeal Chamber should only intervene where the Trial Chamber sentence was so unreasonable or plainly unjust that it's able to infer that the Trial Chamber failed to exercise its discretion properly or - in more descriptive terms - where it was taken from the wrong shelf. That's a high threshold, Your Honours, and rightly so. Trial Chambers have a broad discretion on sentencing. This Trial Chamber had the opportunity to hear the evidence in this case over a period of years, including seeing the video that we were shown today of East Mostar, including hearing directly from the victims of these crimes. Whatever view Your Honours take of the quality of the legal reasoning in relation to the JCE or, we say, the absence of legal reasoning, in relation to the crime base, the Trial Chamber chronicled the crimes painstakingly across thousands of pages of a judgement. Against that background, the Chamber's approach to the gravity of the crimes can't be judged solely in relation to the sentencing section of the judgement; it should be weighed against all the pages previously. We say it can't properly be dismissed as cursory. Do the sentences imposed by this Tribunal in comparable cases compel a conclusion that a 20-year sentence for Stojic would be unjust or plainly unreasonable? They do not, in our submission. Dealing with comparable cases are always problematic. No two cases are truly alike. No comparison will bind Your Honours. And there's another danger that the Defence are conscious of because as soon as I start to compare cases, it would be very easy to suggest that I'm trying to minimise the crimes or trying to minimise our responsibility. Your Honours, that's not my intention. Seeing the videos that the Prosecution showed of East Mostar today hits us even after reading the evidence in this case over so many years; it cannot fail but be deeply affecting. On Stojic's behalf counsel began our submissions last week by extending our sincerest condolences to all the victims of the war in former Yugoslavia, and in so doing he was echoing what Stojic himself said in his statement to the Trial Chamber at the end of closing arguments. He said: "From the bottom of my heart, I would like to say that I sympathise. I feel compassion for those people ... and," he continued, "especially the Muslim victims of that war." It's not our intention, nor his intention, to minimise that suffering. The reference is T52964, beginning at line 25. But we do need to look at past cases in order to try and set out what the range of reasonable sentences might be. And we do maintain, as in paragraphs 210 and 211 of our response, that Djordjevic and Sainovic and relevant. Why those cases? Because they're large JCE cases concerning the expulsion of civilian population on ethnic grounds, hundreds of thousands of civilians were displaced. They can't be dismissed as smaller cases. There was no or extremely limited personal mitigation in those cases. Rather than co-operate with the Tribunal as Stojic did, Djordjevic evaded arrest for four years which prolonged the victims' distress. The sentences in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're looking at the clock. You have got another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELLIS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. The sentences imposed in those cases after appeal ranged from 14 to 22 years, and insofar as that comparison helps in drawing a range -- a bracket of reasonable sentences, they don't suggest that the sentences in this case come from the wrong shelf. The Prosecution argue again today that the Chamber should impose a higher sentence to take account of the gravity of the siege of East Mostar. And in so doing, the Prosecution relied specifically in its reply on the level of criminality reflected in a nine-month campaign of sniping, shelling, and terror. A nine-month campaign, Your Honours, because the siege of East Mostar on the Chamber's findings began in June 1993 an ended in March 1994. But by that time, Stojic was no longer the head of the Defence Department. He left the Defence Department in mid-November 1993. The Trial Chamber say the 15th of November, the Stojic Defence say 10th of November, but for this point it matters not. There was no evidence that he remained a member of the JCE after that point in November 1993. His responsibility stops at that point halfway through the siege of East Mostar. His sentence cannot be based on level of criminality reflected by a nine-month siege, and that's even if Your Honours uphold his conviction for the unlawful infliction of terror on a civilian population, which we invite Your Honours to overturn in the absence of a reasoned finding as to specific intent. In relying on Galic this morning, my learned friends opposite acknowledge that there are differences between that case and this one, and there are important differences. According to Prosecution submissions, the siege of Sarajevo affected about 300.000 civilians. And Galic's responsibility for that siege lasted for a period of 23 months, significantly longer, significantly more civilians than this case. So the comparison offered by the Prosecution does not assist in showing that this sentence in this case was wrong. Your Honour, does the 40-year sentence proposed by the Prosecution fit better? Well, we've tried to set out in our response brief at paragraph 215 the cases in which the Trial Chamber has imposed similar sentences. They don't fit with this case for the reasons given in that brief, but I see that we're out of date now. I see that the Trial Chamber has now passed sentence on Karadzic, and he was sentenced to a 40-year term, the very term that the Prosecution seek in relation to Stojic. He was found to have significantly contributed to a JCE to remove Muslims and Croats from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory, but that's only one aspect of that case. He was also the driving force behind an additional common purpose to take UN personnel hostage. He also significantly contributed to the shelling of Sarajevo, not for months, but for three and a half years. He also significantly contributed to the Srebrenica genocide, which resulted in the death of more than 5.000 men and the transfer of tens of thousands of women, children, and elderly men. Your Honours, Stojic's sentence doesn't belong on the same wall as Karadzic, let alone the same shelf. The increased sentence sought by the Prosecution is dramatic. If the Prosecution appeal is granted, the full term would not expire until 2047, at which point - if alive - Stojic would be 92 years old. We say a sentence of that severity is not warranted. We say the Prosecution have failed to show that the sentence was taken from the wrong shelf, failed to show it was so unreasonable and plainly unjust that it is safe to infer that the Trial Chamber failed to exercise its discretion. And we commend to Your Honours' attention in fact our grounds 56.2 in relation to double counting and 57 in relation to time spent on provisional release with significant restrictions on his liberty. But, Your Honours, this is our final chance to say something to the Bench. We listened closely this morning to the Prosecution say that there were unprecedented -- unprecedented omissions in this judgement and that there were failures to assess all of the evidence in the case. Your Honours, those errors are pervasive. It's the point my learned friend Mr. Karnavas was making I think in the end of his submissions. Those errors are pervasive. They don't stop where the Prosecution appeal finishes. They're symptoms of exactly the same problem that we identified when we said that the Trial Chamber failed to consider the weapons, the munitions in particular, that were sent from Croatia and the HVO - the symptoms of the errors, the failure to consider all of the evidence in relation to the common purpose, single common purpose of the JCE. And, Your Honours, as this hearing has gone on, you've heard more and more errors pointed out by more and more submissions on both sides of the courtroom. And we say the inevitable conclusion at the end of that is unfortunately this is a judgement which does not meet the standards laid down by this Tribunal. It doesn't provide a reasoned decision on all of the evidence, it doesn't assess all of the arguments. And what -- and we say, Your Honours, that the only possible response in the face of all those errors is to reverse the convictions, to allow the Prosecution appeal only to the extent set out in our written brief, and to overturn the conviction of Stojic. Your Honours, think I've used my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ellis. We now move to the Defence team for Mr. Praljak. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I shall be extremely brief. The appeal by the Prosecutor indicates that there are failings in the judgement; this is undeniable. The Prosecutor holds that this is unacceptable as regards a legacy of this Tribunal and of the international community. Today's transcript page 7, line 4 to 5. The judgement in its entirety is indeed full of mistakes which are -- cannot be remedied. Indeed, it is unacceptable. But first and foremost, it is unacceptable for the accused; it is unacceptable for this Tribunal; and lastly, it is unacceptable for international criminal justice, since its credibility is challenged in this case. The first and third ground of the appeal of the Prosecution concerns crimes which would have resulted from the common purpose under Count 1 or that would have been committed as part of a common plan, i.e., third ground of appeal. But there was no common plan. So as regards the first ground of appeal, we cannot talk about a JCE 3 if there is no JCE 1. And as regards or under the third count, we cannot talk about crimes committed as part of a JCE if there is no JCE or JCE does not exist. As regards the remainder, we maintain all our written arguments indicated in our response brief as regards grounds 1, 2, and 3 of the Prosecution. I would just like to add - without addressing what we have already mentioned - one remark concerning the videos we were shown this morning by the Prosecution. These videos make no difference as regards the evidence submitted by the Defence in these proceedings relating to the siege of Mostar. I would invite you to read our grounds of appeal relating to Mostar. Mr. President, Your Honours, we will not submit any arguments concerning ground 4 on sentencing. Any sentencing of Mr. Praljak would be unjust, but first and foremost it would be contrary to the standards and principles -- elementary standards and principles of international law since his responsibility has not been established. The conviction of Mr. Praljak is based on erroneous conclusions, mischaracterised facts, a conclusion which the Trial Chamber reached in which -- after proceedings in which the right of the accused on Article 21 of the Statute was breached. The appeal of the Prosecution should be entirely rejected as well as the arguments -- all the arguments presented by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you okay if we take Petkovic? Yeah, all right. Defence team for Mr. Petkovic. Yes, Defence team for Mr. Petkovic, you can start. Thank you. And you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We're going to try to use our half an hour in the manner we believe to be the best. For a start, I will agree completely with my colleagues from the Prosecution when they said that the judgement is inexplicably inconsistent. I know for a fact that they have spent days and weeks trying to get a grip on what was going on with all 211 incidents and which of the accused was convicted or not convicted for each of one of those incidents. At the start, I'm going talk about appeal ground 2 or the failure by the Chamber to decide the responsibility of the accused according to command responsibility after establishing that there was no responsibility under JCE 3. Slide 2, slide number 2, you can see what the Prosecutor says. I'm going to deal with the request to overturn the judgement and convict my client according -- to counts according to command responsibility, and then I'm going to say a few words about alternative proposals for the Appeals Chamber to overturn this judgement -- or actually, to remand this issue to the Trial Chamber for reconsideration. As far as the acquittal and conviction according to command responsibility, Your Honours, I would like to say that we are aware that I'm embarking on a topic in which this Appeals Chamber holds different views. We know that it's not wise to deal with topics on which there is disagreement among the members of the Trial Chamber, but we will still do that. Slide number 3 is a brief explanation that we require for our submission because in separate opinions of Judge Pocar in the Gotovina case as well as in a series of other cases at this Tribunal, also at the European Court, the position was that an acquittal must not be reversed or overturned, regardless of the discretion of the Chamber to do so, if thereby they deny the accused's right to an appeal. Since the Statute or the Rules of this Court do not foresee an appeal to an appeal decision, then it's a question whether in such a case the right of our accused would be violated, i.e., for a higher court to review a judgement reached in such a way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please speak -- slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will do. In view of the fact that I'm also focussed on human rights, this standpoint is very dear to me. I would like to point out what the practice was in the former Yugoslavia 50 years ago. The following slides show an excerpt on the Law on Criminal Procedure of the SFRY. The year is 1986, but this is a law from 1977 that has been revised. And you can see from this text that this law during the time of Yugoslavia, which was a single-party Communist totalitarian country, accused had the right to appeal against the verdict of a court in the second instance and is ruled on in the third instances only in the following cases. If the court in the second instance modified a verdict of acquittal of the court in the first instance and pronounced a verdict finding the accused guilty, all of this was very well conceived. The Law on Criminal Procedure today of the Republic of Croatia contains the same wording. This is Article 490 of the law. Also, this is contained in the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They included this right at the beginning of the 1990s because all the countries created from the former Yugoslavia inherited the Law on Criminal Procedure, and this provision is contained in the criminal procedure law of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the moment. In our countries, had this trial been conducted in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, our appeal -- our appellants would be guaranteed the right not to have an acquittal turned into a conviction without assuring the adequate protection, meaning the appeal to -- the right to appeal and for a higher court to review the legality of a decision by a higher court. What we expected from you, Your Honours, was to provide equal rights to our accused before this Tribunal as the ones they would have had, had they been tried according to the laws of the former state which was a single-party Communist totalitarian state. As for our alternative request for the case to be -- to be re-tried, here we have explicitly heard of one crime that my client is being charged with in that context, that is the murder of six detainees in Dretelj. My colleague Ms. Baig mentioned four such crimes. I think that this was an error because our records indicate that there was six killings. In the column we have tried to show what the Trial Chamber's conclusions were regarding that incident and why it did not convict Petkovic under JCE 3 of liability. The Trial Chamber believed that Petkovic was informed about the event seven months after the event, and therefore that was not something that was foreseeable as far as he was concerned. The next column we have two brief paragraphs from the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecutor considers that the factual conclusions of the Trial Chamber are sufficient to overturn an acquittal into a conviction. Just a brief comment. Now I'm going to try to be very, very fast. The whole story is based actually on a document by the International Red Cross, P07636, which is the source of Petkovic's information about the crime. The slide will present this document. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the document was set to Mr. Marjan Biskic and it states here that he was the deputy minister of defence. He was actually assistant minister. And for our purposes today, it is important that this was a person who was in charge at the Ministry of Defence for the military police and the security service called SIS, S-I-S, who was responsible for processing perpetrators of crimes and for conducting investigations. Thus, he was the one who received this letter which was sent for the information to Petkovic, Prlic, and to the president's office and to the Supreme Command. If we keep in mind some other circumstances that I'm referring to here, and because I have such a brief period of time at my disposal I'm only going to refer to 4D01614. The document clearly indicates that Petkovic, although at that time in December 1993 was deputy head of the HVO Main Staff, was not automatically the person in charge if the chief of the HVO Main Staff was absent. We see from the document that Ante Roso who was the then-head of the Main Staff said that other than Petkovic Matic, Vrbanac were also authorised to stand in for him when he was absent. So if we established who at which period was authorised to carry out the tasks of the chief of the Main Staff, we need to be familiar with a whole series of circumstances. At this point I don't want to burden you with the regulations dealing with who was in charge and how to discipline soldiers; we don't have time for that. But based on this, in brief, I can conclude in view of the fact that a person authorised to process crime perpetrators was informed about the crime and was authorised to undertake the necessary steps, there was no reason for Petkovic, Prlic, or the Supreme Commander do anything in particular in that regard. The next slide, slide number 9 refers to the thefts in Stupni Do for which the Prosecution also cites Petkovic's responsibility according to the chain of command. I'm going to try to be as brief as possible here because there's a lot of information that I wanted to go over. The crime did happen; that is beyond dispute. We discussed this in our submissions last Thursday, but what we would like to say is -- can we please look at the next slide and can it please not be broadcast because it contains statements by protected witnesses, so I just wanted to make sure that they remain confidential. As for the investigation itself, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: (redacted) Witness Bandic spoke about the activities of the military prosecutor. This is transcript 38101. Witness Jan Koet confirmed his contacts with the public prosecutor regarding the accusations regarding crimes in Stupni Do. This is P10092, paragraph 22. Engaging the military district prosecutor involved to investigate the crimes in Stupni Do is seen on the basis of document 4D00499. Ivica Rajic who led the actions in Vares explicitly communicated with the Supreme Commander Mate Boban, and the following evidence speaks as to that. (redacted) Ivica Rajic sent reports directly to the Supreme Commander. Exhibit P06291. Boban spoke about the crimes in Stupni Do, the investigations, and the necessity to punish the perpetrators at a meeting with President Tudjman in Split on the 5th of November, 1993. My client, General Petkovic, was also present. This is the document P06575. Then-Defence Minister Perica Jukic contacted UNPROFOR in order to investigate the crimes in Stupni Do. This is document 4D00506. And now we can show the next slide and then we will keep the following one confidential. This is evidence that speaks about the security service, the SIS, and the one that investigated the crimes in Stupni Do. This is document P06828. It's a SIS report which was sent to the then-Minister of Defence Jukic and the then-Chief of the HVO Main Staff Roso. Witness Bandic also spoke about this. This is transcript 38324. Witness Jan Koet? Also spoke about the investigation, same document, P10092. If we accept the standard set by the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic judgement, we are going to see that the organs authorised to investigate and process perpetrators of crimes were absolutely involved in relation to Stupni Do. Other than that, at that point in time, Petkovic was the deputy chief of the Main Staff, and I just need a couple of more minutes to discuss how Ivica Rajic changed his name to Viktor Andric. Can we please not broadcast this slide. We can see from the following documents that on the 10th of November, 1993, Mate Boban issued a statement that Rajic was relieved of duty. This is document P10255. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: (redacted) This is transcript 24532 to 323 (as interpreted). Witness Bandic told us that Mate Boban decided to keep Rajic but under the name of Viktor Andric. This is transcript page 38306. And now there's a series of documents - I mentioned just a few here - but there are numerous such documents showing that the entire political and military structure of Herceg-Bosna knew that Rajic had changed his name. I apologise if somebody perhaps didn't even know that, but my client, Mr. Petkovic, did know that. And then what happened then with Ivica Rajic? In April 1994 again he changed his name to Jakov Kovac this time. In 1995 Rajic was arrested but he was not charged for the crimes in Stupni Do, and finally the Mostar Court acquitted Rajic. All this evidence and there are more, we can conclude that Milivoj Petkovic cannot be held responsibility according to command responsibility for the theft in Stupni Do. Simply speaking, all his superiors were equally as informed about all events, and the organs of Herceg-Bosna entrusted with the investigation and processing of crimes were informed about everything. The conclusion about this is that we feel that this ground should be denied as groundless. As for the third ground of appeal, just briefly, I really tried and read the judgement a million times. And in my view and according to my reading of judgement, the Prosecution is not correct when they say that my client was not convicted of wilful destruction, wanton destruction, in these four locations. In the left-hand column you see which locations are dealt with here. I also tried to give excerpts from volumes 3 and 4, the paragraphs that refer to those crimes, and my conclusion is that my client was punished. Perhaps this is one more proof of how hard it is to read this judgement. I think that I still have -- I just have five minutes, ah, ten minutes. Ten minutes. Then I can slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct, you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to talk about the first ground of appeal, and I'm going to round off with the topic of Mostar and the sentencing. As for the first ground of appeal is concerned, the Prosecution stated correctly that there is a total lack of uniformity as far as terminology is concerned. We tried to determine when probability and possibility standards are being used. For our purposes here, General Petkovic, we believe that the standard has been properly set and established, and we believe that there is a lot of linguistic confusion here and that in essence the real, proper standard was applied; and that for this reason, this ground of appeal is without basis. As for analysing the crime base in such a way that each individual crime is separately analysed, we hope that as in the judgements -- in the judgement case, paragraph 413 and Martic appeal, paragraph 169, we believe that an analysis should be carried out on a case-by-case basis. I will skip a couple of sides now because I don't have sufficient time. We will continue at page 20. I am very happy when I come across a situation where I can agree with the Prosecution and thank them for something they have done for my client, as I would like to do so now. According to their ground of appeal 1(g) under (f), they were of the belief that General Petkovic was convicted for destructing religious facilities under JCE 1, but it should have been under JCE 3. Given the fact that this works in favour of my client, I would like to thank them; but we nevertheless believe that there is no ground for liability under any of these aspects. Given the fact that my learned friends concluded their presentation by showing video footage of Mostar, which is upsetting enough, I also wanted to conclude my presentation discussing the siege of Mostar, its destruction and the terror of civilians. We can play the footage now. It is slide 21. We do not want to diminish the importance of any victim. What we wanted to provide the Appeals Chamber with, according to our view, is a full picture of events. All of these people were protected witnesses, meaning that the transcript provided here is also protected. These three witnesses, Your Honours, were the representatives of the international community: Witnesses BB, BA, and BC. If you look again at what they said on the topic, we can see that they established that the civilians could and wanted to leave East Mostar but were not allowed by their authorities, the statements of these three witnesses are identical. They also referred the Bench to their reports. In other words, they were aware of the situation, i.e., that the civilians wanted to leave East Mostar. We also wanted to specify a couple of Army of BiH documents, meaning the people from their hierarchy who were placed there East Mostar. Document 4D719 is dated the 14th of October, 1993. It is a report by the commander of the ABiH. He said that transporting the civilian population presents a great problem as well as the transport of others leaving in the direction east and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: North and south of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this was in October of 1993. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted the civilian authorities to assume the proper role and take responsibility for transport of civilians. The next document is 4D545, an excerpt from Esad Sejtanic's book. He was an ABiH commander. He literally wrote as follows: "Many inhabitants want to go to Jablanica and further afield to Bosnia. By repressive measures regrettably, we prevented the outflow of population and reduced any movement of population to a minimum." Your Honours, we wanted to show you this, so as to keep in mind that the situation in Mostar was not only the consequence of operations conducted by the HVO. The ABiH was very much active in the area at that time as well. As can you see, civilians remained in East Mostar, also because the authorities in that part of town would not allow them to leave. Believing, Your Honours, that we managed to show that in the first half of 1993 there were no mass movements of Muslims and that no crime committed during that time can be reasonably concluded as a crime having being committed with the idea of furthering the plan of ethnic cleansing, and given that in mid-1993 there was an all-out war between the HVO and the ABiH, and that the so-called siege of Mostar and the plight of civilians came as a result of not only HVO actions but those of the ABiH as well, primarily because they prohibited the civilians to leave East Mostar - bearing all that in mind, as we specified in our submissions, we believe that my client's sentence, the sentence of General Petkovic, is not unreasonable or unjust from the point of view as discussed by the Prosecution. It should not be increased. It should either be reversed, rejected, or drastically reduced. Thank you very much. I believe I have run out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. We will have an hour-and-a-half break instead of the one hour that was communicated to you. So we will resume at 15 minutes past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So thank you. Mr. -- Defence for Mr. Coric, you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. At this time we would like to try to utilize that time-period which we have as efficiently as possible. Since we already addressed the Prosecution's ground 1A last week in -- at some great length in response to Your Honours' questions, I believe it was question 10, we will not be spending more time on that today repeating those same arguments. Instead we will focus more on the remaining grounds of the Prosecution appeal. We also announce that we stand behind our written submissions such that we are not conceding anything -- any topic that is in our written submissions which we do not get to discuss in open court today due to the time. In essence, the Prosecution appeal presented in its brief and today presents several grounds seeking an increase of a sentence which we believe is already manifestly in excess and unjust given the circumstances. The Prosecution relies upon Mr. Coric's position and alleged acts and omissions to allow a climate of impunity, and we submit that when viewed under the totality of the evidence as the trial -- pardon me, as the Prosecution even asked Your Honours to do at temporary transcript page 12, lines 14 to 25, as to Coric, we believe that under that totality the conclusions of the Prosecution are wrong as to Mr. Coric. I will just say a few words about subground 1B of the Prosecution appeal. The Prosecution claims that the Trial Chamber disregarded Prosecution evidence and thus wrongfully acquitted Mr. Coric of certain incidents. However, the Prosecution has failed to show what evidence was alleged to be in existence which was disregarded and which showed that Coric knew of the commission of crimes and that he was involved in the crimes and that he also knew that they were not being punished or processed by the relevant investigative or judicial entity. To the contrary, a review of the judgement and the underlying evidence demonstrates that it was Defence evidence on this matter that was not engaged and properly analysed by the Chamber and which now must be analysed in light of the Prosecution's appeal. At paragraph 29 of our response to the appeal, we have detailed certain evidence that the Trial Chamber disregarded from the Defence, including court registers of hundreds of criminal reports filed by both the military and civilian police against perpetrators of crimes against Muslim victims. Now you may ask why is that important. Let me bring that to your attention. Today at temporary transcript page 4, we heard the Prosecution's very emotive rendering of the events surrounding the tragic death and murder of Sanida Kaplan. And I apologise if the pronunciation of the name is off, I'm not sure exactly if it is Kaplan or Kaplan, but that is the individual at issue. I would direct Your Honours to the evidence in the case, P9550, 5D4234, P -- pardon me, 5D4236. These are precisely court proceedings, indeed judgements, that have been entered against the perpetrators of the crimes relating to the Kaplan family entered by the appropriate organs in BiH. And furthermore, if one reads those judgements, you will see that the judicial authorities after the war cite to and are greatly assisted by criminal reports and other documents that date from 1993 that are precisely part of these court registers that the Defence has been talking about that were transferred to the relevant judicial organs to complete the investigative work that had been accomplished by the police filing criminal reports against perpetrators. And that is the -- the register we've been talking about is 5D4288. We have discussed it at length. This is a large number of proceedings for crimes against persons of all ethnicities. So, Your Honours, we submit that the Prosecution was not entirely correct this morning when they left Your Honours with the impression that justice would be denied to the Kaplan family if these acquittals of Mr. Coric were to stand. Indeed, justice against the actual persons who committed the crimes has already been undertaken by the organs at issue. And there's been no linkage to any acts or omissions of Mr. Coric. Thus, we submit, the Prosecution appeal has no merit if we consider this bulk of evidence that supports the proper processing of criminal reports by both the military and civilian police, and, therefore, the acquittal of Coric should be for even more crimes than those that the Trial Chamber acquitted him of. Given the presumption of innocence and the requirements of in dubio pro reo and given that the Prosecution bears the burden of proof, we believe that any error made by the Chamber needs to be again evaluated by this Appeals Chamber under the light of those same principles, and in that sense, the Prosecution ground cannot be sustained. I would move to ground 2 of the Prosecution's appeal relating to Article 7(3) responsibility. Your Honours have read in regards to ground 2 of the appeal that the Prosecution focuses this ground on their brief that Mr. Coric had effective control over military policemen and that he was an architect, as they say in paragraph 404 of their appeal, of the HVO network of detention centres. And we've heard a lot today about this network of HVO detention centres. In fact, I was able to mark down at least at temporary transcript page 32 and 36 that the Prosecutor relied upon that network today. And they claim that Mr. Coric failed to do anything to punish or prevent crimes. This morning, Your Honours, at temporary transcript page 17, they claimed that Mr. Coric, among others, had knowledge of crimes, and then at temporary transcript page 14, they said he did not take steps to curb criminality. We believe that the evidence and the incidents that the Prosecution relies upon do not support this conclusion. And as an example, one incident relied upon by the Prosecution in its appeal brief, and they use this for both JCE 3 and 7(3) liability of Mr. Coric, is the 14 July 1993 incident involving the killing of one and the wounding of two detainees at Dretelj. And this is at Prosecution appeal brief, paragraph 279, and 317 through 321. However, if the facts of the same are review -- are dilated upon, it is clear that no 7(3) command responsibility nor other criminal liability can be attributed to Mr. Coric. And, again, Dretelj was mentioned at temporary transcript page 20 today, albeit in a general sense as to another appellant. Now, in the Prosecution's appeal, they rely upon P3446 in footnote 1016 for this ground. But that document, from the commander of the military police stationed at Dretelj, claims as to the perpetrator, a Mr. Vulic, a military policemen who shot the inmates as follows: "After giving a statement was then relieved of his duty as military policeman, crime investigators will conduct a more detailed investigation about all of this." That's what the document the Prosecution relies upon says. It is clear from such a report that Mr. Coric as chief of the military police administration was informed that after a shooting incident, all necessary and appropriate steps foreseen under the law were taken by the authorities, indeed by the superior officer of the perpetrator, who had possibly committed a crime and that steps were under way by the investigative organs to determine the consequences of the same. There was no reason for Mr. Coric to doubt that all appropriate investigative and disciplinary procedures, including legal steps, would be taken according to the relevant authorities after having received that report. Thus, Coric could not be put on notice of any crime for which he needed to intervene to punish or discipline himself. Indeed, we have other evidence, P3476, and a Prosecution protected witness who testified at 22401 to 22402 as to appropriate steps that were taken against the perpetrator of this shooting. Now, under the prevailing ICTY jurisprudence, where reports were made to the appropriate authorities by subordinates of the accused for the institution of disciplinary matters, the accused has discharged his duty and cannot be held criminally responsible under Article 3. We have that from the Boskoski and Tarculovski trial judgement, paragraph 536. Further, we have from the Popovic appeals judgement, paragraph 1942, that the use of disciplinary measures may be sufficient for a superior to discharge his duty to punish crimes under Article 7(3). As we stressed last week and as we stress again here today, neither Coric nor the military police could undertake steps once a criminal investigation and criminal report were submitted to the relevant judicial organs to follow through on the initial disciplinary actions of military policemen who may have committed crimes. Contrary to what the Prosecution presents in their appeal, Coric had no effective control over military policemen at Dretelj and Gabela military remand prisons which were under the effective command and control of the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade and its commander, Obradovic. We see that at P3731, P4253. The evidence shows the sole duty of the military police battalion within Dretelj was to assist the HVO brigade in security issues under the command of the brigade commander and to report on eventual criminal incidents connected to murders of the military police. The evidence shows the military police administration did not have and Mr. Coric did not have authority nor influence over the conditions of detention at these two facilities. Now, this relates to what the Prosecution said today at temporary transcript page 17 and 14 as to steps not being taken by Coric to curb criminality. In our response brief to the Prosecution appeal, at paragraphs 52 and 81 through 83, we showed the variety and multitude of steps that Mr. Coric undertook, his many efforts to try to positively affect conditions in Dretelj despite his lack of authority over the same, by addressing various higher organs. We will not repeat those submissions here today, but, rather, would refer Your Honours to look to those sections of our response brief and consider those paragraphs and consider those efforts of Coric when assessing whether the Prosecution's claim, as presented today, bears merit or, as we submit, does not bear merit. We submit that no Article 7(3) command liability can attach to Mr. Coric for failing to take actions within his limited powers, especially under the existing evidence on record. And, again, Your Honours at temporary transcript page 10, lines 10 through 19, and temporary transcript page 12, lines 14 to 25, Madam Prosecutors asked that the Trial Chamber needed to look at the totality of the evidence. We believe if Your Honours look at the totality of the evidence, you will agree that Mr. Coric cannot bear criminal responsibility for these incidents. Now, again, as an extension of this same point and again responding to paragraph 404 of the Prosecution's appeal wherein Mr. Coric is named as an architect of this network of detention centres which was mentioned today at least two or three times, I have temporary transcript pages 32 and 36 written down, and today also the Prosecution said that the Trial Chamber erroneously acquitted Mr. Coric despite having made findings that he should have been found guilty of. Well, if we use this same standard to review the trial judgement, the Defence submits that exculpatory findings and contradictory conclusions of the Trial Chamber are made as to Coric in finding him guilty. We would point out, among other things, the following. Volume 4, paragraphs 905, 916, 1421, 1428 of the judgement, wherein Coric never restricted access to representatives of international organisations when requested. This doesn't fit into the Prosecution's scenario as presented today. Therefore, their appeal cannot stand. Next, volume 4, paragraph 955, the Trial Chamber found that Coric was not informed of mistreatment and had no reason to believe detainees were mistreated. This also does not support the Prosecution appeal today. Volume 2, paragraph 1470, finding that beginning October 1992, there is no evidence that detainees were sent to perform labour with Coric's approval. Volume 2, paragraph 1612, 1617, 1633, that neither the military police administration nor the military police were involved in any incident inducing the alleged mistreatment of detainees working in the front lines. We believe that Your Honours should also look at the contradictory finding of the Trial Chamber at volume 2, 1446, insisting that Coric ordered release of detained persons upon letters of guarantee despite confirming that no such orders existed in evidence. And we would also point to the -- volume 4, paragraph 960 to 961, that restrictions or obstructions to access to the detention centres could not be said to be ordered by Coric. And just two more. Volume 4, 897, 899, and paragraphs 955, 957, 962, 985, 988, 1018, that demonstrate that Coric lacked access to reports about prison conditions. Again, this does not support the version of events that the Prosecution has presented as part of their appeal today. And lastly, in this regard, volume 4, 904, the finding that Coric was not involved in health matters or logistics for the prisons which, again, goes contrary to the Prosecution's appeal. Respectfully, if the Prosecution wishes to look at the Trial Chamber's errors, it must concede that these errors apply to the convictions of Mr. Coric as to detention facilities. Thus, we believe that to grant the Prosecution appeal one would have to ignore these other inconsistencies and these false convictions which would thus lead to a miscarriage of justice. As to ground 3 of the Prosecution's appeal, I think we have been rather clear and succinct in our response brief and therefore we stand upon what is written therein and direct Your Honours to consider the same. I then move to ground 4, sentencing. And Your Honours have heard today from the Prosecution that these sentences, and in particular the sentence against Mr. Coric, were manifestly insufficient or inadequate. I have recorded down at least four times when that was said. Temporary transcript page 26, 27, 31, and 32. Your Honours, Mr. Coric received a 16-year sentence. In paragraph 137 to 140 of our response brief, we have pointed out that this sentence is indeed in excess of the maximum sentence that was available to be issued under the existing SFRY and SRBiH law at the time of the alleged offences that formed the conviction. Thus, it is inappropriate to call such a sentence "manifestly insufficient." And I know although the Tribunal has decided that it is not bound by the SFRY sentencing provisions, we would draw Your Honours' attention to international law and the principle of nullum crimen sine lege, nulla poena sine lege. The law in force at the time of the commission of the crimes alleged was the 1976 Criminal Code which remained authoritative in BiH until after the year 2000. It dictated that war crimes were to be punished by imprisonment that falls within five to 15 years or by the death penalty for most crimes, but the death penalty was abolished and substituted by the possibility to impose a 20-year term. You can see this from Articles 38, 142 and 37 of the relevant law. The prohibition on retroactivity inherently implies a prohibition on the retroactive application of the lex gravior, i.e., the more severe penalty. Consequently, it is unlawful to impose a heavier penalty which did not exist at the material time of the commission of the crimes and the lesser sentence should be applied as per the favor libertatis principle. Now, Your Honours, that's not just a submission of the Defence. That is a holding of the European Court of Human Rights in Maktouf and Damjanovic v. BiH, page 11. The principle of legality and its corollary nulla poena sine lege inherently imply a prohibition on the application of a more stringent penal code than that which existed at the time of commission. We submit that the prohibition on retroactivity is part of customary international law and a preemptory norm of international law permitting no derogations. That's what the European of Court of Human Rights in Maktouf and Damjanovic v BiH said at page 46. So thus in dealing with the same issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have four minutes left, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In dealing with the same issue, an application of the 2003 BiH Criminal Code instead of the 1976 SFRY one, the European Court of Human Rights found that it was a violation to apply the newer law which had more stringent sentences than the prior law. Under such a backdrop, this sentence against Mr. Coric cannot be found manifestly inadequate. For this reason alone we would ask that Your Honours should not increase the sentence but should lower the same. But we have also addressed other arguments in our response brief which I will not take the time to go through in detail but we believe each of them calls for a reduction in sentence or indeed no sentence, not an increase, irrespective of whether you accept the argument and holding of the European Court of Human Rights. Today Madam Prosecutor mentioned several other ICTY cases. We have already dealt with those in paragraphs 129 through 133 of our response and stand on those submissions. We also join in the submissions made today by Mr. Ellis of the Stojic Defence as to sentencing and will not repeat the same. We saw a very emotive video today. And war, unfortunately, leads to victims and it leads to emotions, and we believe that Your Honours should view the law, view the facts absent emotion and should judge based upon the evidence that we believe shows that Mr. Coric, from his position, tried to act as an honourable police enforcement official, first at the military police administration and later at the civilian MUP, and he tried to prevent crimes and bring perpetrators to justice by way of filing criminal reports and taking other steps. And, therefore, we reject the Prosecution's appeal that he should be convicted and that his sentence should be further increased. Thank you, Your Honours. I hope that I have stayed within my time-limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did, Mr. Ivetic, and I thank you. It is now the turn of the Defence team of Mr. Pusic. Are you comfortable there, Mr. Sahota, or do you wish to come in front?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Go ahead then. You have 30 minutes starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend now to address you on the aspects of the Prosecution's appeal which directly impinge and are relevant to my client Mr. Pusic. As we tried yesterday, we will take the same approach. We will endeavor to accept points made by the Prosecution where that's appropriate, we will endeavour to adopt submissions made by other parties where that is appropriate. The theme of our submissions yesterday was that Mr. Pusic was not a high-level official and was a -- one of the accused that should be treated differently. And one way we say that point is reinforced in these appeal proceedings is that he is the only defendant who was not convicted of JCE 3, and it follows that he is the only defendant for which the Prosecution say the Trial Chamber's decision should be reversed and his acquittals reversed. Your Honours, I'll start by addressing with you on ground 1 of the Prosecution's appeal brief. Very briefly, I would touch on the propositions made as to the correct mens rea standard for JCE 3. In short, we say that the position adopted by the Prosecution is erroneous. We're not going to rehearse the points made earlier today by the Stojic Defence. We will simply say that the test of foreseeability that this Chamber should adopt and the Trial Chamber should have implemented, did implement, we say, involves a subjective element. The Court has to consider the possibility that the crime could have been committed as sufficiently substantial so as to be foreseeable to the accused based on the information available to him. Your Honours, two points arise from that statement of the law. Firstly, as articulated by the Stojic Defence earlier today, the threshold is not so low as just to trigger criminal liability on the basis that the accused should have seen a certain event was possible. The second point that arises is that the foreseeability test should be individually tailored to the accused. There are individually specific factors that should be considered, including, and not just limited to, the location of the accused at any point during the time on the indictment. Your Honours, we intend to apply that individual -- individually tailored, specific foreseeability test to the evidence that is cited by the Prosecution as, in their opinion, establishing Mr. Pusic's guilt for deviatory JCE 3 crimes. Your Honours, at this juncture I would also ask you to note what is also accepted as the law on JCE 3, that depending on the information available to accused, what may be foreseeable to one accused as a member of the JCE may not be foreseeable to another. Applying that -- the correct test, we say there is nothing wrong with the Trial Chamber's findings. We say that the fact that Mr. Pusic was acquitted of all JCE 3 crimes should not be interfered with. Your Honours, this morning you heard the Prosecution make reference to 33 individual JCE 3 findings where the Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion. I will refer to these as the remaining crimes and they're the crimes which are addressed by the Prosecution in their appeal brief at pages 112 to 116. We say what explains the Trial Chamber's decision to acquit Mr. Pusic of all these JCE 3 crimes is the paucity of evidence linking him to these events. The Chamber made very limited findings, often it made no findings at all, in relation to Mr. Pusic's responsibility for these matters because there was no evidence connecting him to these events. They certainly didn't find any evidence of any link between Mr. Pusic and the perpetrators of these 33 JCE 3 crimes. Your Honours, nonetheless, it's the position of the Prosecution that Mr. Pusic should be liable under the JCE 3 theory for these deviatory acts, these individual wayward actions outside the shared intent. Your Honours, I would ask the Appeals Chamber to reflect on whether that can be right as a proposition of facts applied to the law. When you have heard what we've said about Mr. Pusic's role, he's different, when you've heard what we've said about Mr. Pusic's powers and the inconclusive evidence as to the extent of those powers, is it really correct that despite there being any evidence linking him to the perpetrators of these crimes in most of these 33 different instances, that those crimes should have been foreseeable to him? Is this a finding that can properly be made to the criminal standard beyond a reasonable doubt? Your Honours, I'll turn now briefly to other crimes which are more specifically addressed by the Prosecution at subground 1A(ii) and (iii), pages 110 to 111 of the Prosecution's appeal brief. In these instances there are slightly more detailed factual findings that the Prosecution is in a position to address. When we examine these specific factual findings, we say that the Appeals Chamber should decide that the Trial Chamber rightly held that they did not warrant a conviction under JCE 3. Turning, first of all, to the Prosecution's appeal concerning the crimes that led to the destruction of the mosques in Sovici and Doljani, page 110 of their appeal brief, applying the individually tailored foreseeability test, noting that the offences in question took place in the same month the Chamber found that Mr. Pusic joined the JCE. We're talking about April 1993. Noting that the evidence that is cited by the OTP merely shows that Mr. Pusic learned of the destruction of the mosques ex post facto after the event. After the event. Your Honours, that, we would suggest, is not on its own or taken with other evidence of context sufficient for any court to decide that that crime would have been foreseeable to him. Moving on to the Prosecution's submissions concerning Vojno. This is ground 1A(ii), paragraphs 250 to -1 of the Prosecution's appeal brief. The Prosecution's position is that Mr. Pusic should be convicted applying JCE 3 liability of the killing of a detainee at the Vojno detention centre. They similarly rely on the fact that he knew about this killing, but the position is that he only learnt of this fatality many months after the event. Your Honours, we say that whether you look at that evidence on its own or if you look at it taking into account globally what the Prosecution say about his role, what the findings are on JCE 1, it does not justify a finding that that particular fatality would have been foreseeable to him applying the individually tailored foreseeability test. Your Honours, in respect of both these incidents, the Prosecution place great emphasis on the general evidence of Mr. Pusic's knowledge, his role, his powers, all the facts related to his conviction under JCE 1, and there are large tracts from the Trial Chamber's decision that are cited in the reasoning provided by the Prosecution. Your Honours, what they ask is that you should make a specific finding that these crimes were foreseeable to Mr. Pusic based largely on general evidence that these crimes were foreseeable. Your Honours, in summary, our position is that there is an insufficient basis, an insufficient basis in logic and an insufficient basis in law upon which this Chamber should impute criminal responsibility applying JCE 3 to Mr. Pusic for these extended and deviatory crimes. We say that what the Prosecution is effectively inviting you to do is to adopt what my learned friend for Mr. Stojic called this morning an open-ended foreseeability test. What they are asking you to do is to apply too low a threshold for finding intent. If you choose to adopt this course of action what in effect will be happening is that the Chamber will be casting the net so wide insofar as determining liability for deviatory crimes that JCE theory as applied in this case would achieve the opposite effect of what was intended by the Tadic Appeal Chamber. Your Honours, I'll refer you to a quite famous quote from the Tadic appeal judgement, I'm sure you're familiar with it. I'm sure it's been rehearsed before you on many occasions. Paragraph 428: "... joint criminal enterprise is not an open-ended concept that permits convictions based on guilt by association." Your Honours, in regard to this specific limb of their appeal, ground 1, we say the Prosecution have failed to eliminate reasonable doubt that these deviatory crimes were foreseeable to Mr. Pusic, a low-ranking HVO official, which is all the evidence shows. I'm going to conclude very quickly by briefly addressing you on ground 4. Your Honours, the Prosecution asked you to enhance the sentence that was imposed by the Trial Chamber of ten years imprisonment. They do not -- and I adopt the submissions of the Stojic Defence, I think what was said this morning applies equally to Mr. Pusic. We do not accept that they have failed to identify any material error on the part of the Chamber in the approach that was adopted when to came to determining sentence. We also adopt what was said about the Trial Chamber's -- the Prosecution's failure to demonstrate that the sentence imposed is manifestly unfair or plainly unjust and meets the criteria set out in the Galic appeals judgement. What a reading of the Prosecution appeal brief really demonstrates is their unhappiness and discontent at the sentences imposed in general. Your Honours, the Prosecution asked that Mr. Pusic's sentence be enhanced because they claim that the sentence does not reflect his degree of participation in the JCE. You heard yesterday what they had to say. They claimed that he a key role in detention centres. They claim that he had a key role in releases and evacuations of prisoners despite the fact, we say, that there was evidence adduced that was ignored in the Trial Chamber's decision that these orders were made by others higher up the food-chain and also that these evacuations and releases often took place with the involvement of organisations such as the ECMM and the ICRC. Your Honours, I will conclude by saying this. The Prosecution asked for a sentence of 20 years to be substituted for the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber. Our simple reply is this, that this would be wholly and unjustifiably disproportionate in the circumstances based on the evidence that is before you and is referred to in detail in the Trial Chamber's decision. For these reasons, Your Honours, we ask that the Appeals Chamber dismisses the arguments advanced in the Prosecution's appeal insofar as they impact on Mr. Pusic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sahota. That brings us to the Prosecution. You have 30 minutes, Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Just for the record, I would like to mention that we have been joined by an additional colleague, Ms. Sarah Houlihan. In his arguments this morning, counsel for Mr. Stojic falls into the same trap as the Trial Chamber by favouring location-specific factors at the expense of factors that show that Stojic was well aware of the nature and scale of the common criminal purpose. Stojic's foresight of JCE 3 crimes does not depend on any municipality-specific factors that the Defence have alluded to this morning. This argument is supported neither by the facts nor the law. The law is clear that an accused's foresight of possible JCE 3 crimes depends on the totality of the circumstances surrounding the implementation of the common purpose. And the accused's participation in it. And that's Sainovic appeals judgement. It does not support a compartmentalised location-specific approach. None of the factors set out in the prior jurisprudence of this Tribunal, none of those indicators are location specific. None require the ability to predict where and when the JCE 3 crime might occur. And on the facts, the Defence has not pointed to anything that would support assessing Stojic or any of the other respondents' ability to foresee JCE 3 crimes based only on their knowledge and involvement in a specific municipality in question. To the contrary, Your Honours. Each of the respondents shared a common purpose to commit a consistent pattern of crimes across Herceg-Bosna in order to render this territory ethnically homogeneous. And each of them played a role in the JCE that related to its implementation across Herceg-Bosna territory. Stojic, I would remind you, was the head of the Defence Department for the Herceg-Bosna government. And from this senior position, he was found to have played a key role in implementing the common criminal purpose throughout Herceg-Bosna territory. For Stojic, just as for the other respondents in light of the central roles that they played, it would make no sense to assess their ability to foresee the possible commission of JCE 3 crimes based only on their knowledge and involvement of crimes in a particular municipality where the crimes occurred. Counsel also falls into the trap of focusing on actual knowledge of past crimes which is not required for joint criminal enterprise 3 liability. But where actual knowledge or notice does exist as it does in many instances in this case, it is certainly relevant. And there were reports that were personally addressed to Stojic. And to give you just one more example in addition to Siljeg's report, Exhibit P2770. And you heard about this report last week. It was sent to Stojic on 14 June 1993. It contained information about rapes, forcible moves into apartments, beatings, and "indications of new murders of civilians" that accompanied eviction operations in West Mostar. That's notice before all but two of the JCE 3 murder incidents that the Prosecution has appealed. It is information about rapes prior to any of the incidents of sexual violence that the Prosecution has appealed. And that's information about theft before all but one of the JCE 3 incidents that the Prosecution has appealed. With regard to a few matters raised by the Petkovic Defence. In relation to the number of Dretelj detainees for my argument on ground 2, the Defence is correct: In ground 2, the Prosecution is requesting that Petkovic be convicted for the murder and wilful killing of six rather than four detainees at Dretelj prison. And with regard to the thefts in Stupni Do. The Defence's list of measures taken in response to thefts and other crimes in Stupni Do ignores how Petkovic covered up these crimes by instructing Rajic to conduct a sham investigation, as Mr. Schneider discussed last week. Nor could Petkovic rely on others to take measures to address these crimes, as the Defence has argued today, given his awareness that Boban and others were also trying to protect Rajic. As the Appeals Chamber has held in other cases, a superior cannot rely on a particular measure if he know it is likely to trigger a sham investigation. And I'd refer you to Boskoski appeals judgement paragraph 234. And that's exactly what happened here. And just to clarify one further point about Petkovic's authority at the time he received the ICRC letter, P7636. At that time Petkovic was the deputy chief of the HVO Main Staff, and as Mr. Schneider explained last week, at that time he retained his effective control over HVO forces. Exhibit 4D1614 cited by the Defence today does not undermine the Chamber's findings on this point. With regard to submissions on behalf of Mr. Coric. First concerning the convictions in relation to the Kaplan murder and the crimes at that time in the same village, the two documents that Coric's Defence has referred to relate to criminal proceedings in 1997 and 2004. The Chamber addressed the issue of the filing of criminal reports at volume 1, paragraphs 918 and 919, and volume 4, paragraphs 880 and 882, and properly found that Coric failed to address crimes including eviction and detention-related crimes. Your Honours, what is important here is that the fact that there's an investigation and potentially even criminal responsibility later does not affect -- does not tell us anything about a particular accused's ability to foresee that the crimes would have occurred in the first place. So this sort of action taken long after the fact tells us nothing about the foreseeability of the crimes. And at temporary transcript page 85, in relation to Heliodrom, Coric's counsel has again claimed that "the Chamber even found Coric was not informed of mistreatment and had no reason to believe detainees were mistreated." Again, the paragraph that he cites, volume 4, paragraph 955, finds the opposite. And I quote: "Valentin Coric had reason to believe that the Heliodrom detainees were being mistreated during detention." That's clear in both the English and the French versions of the judgement. Finally, Coric has claimed that he took adequate steps upon learning of the killings in Dretelj in 1993. We've set out our response for this, for example, in the Prosecution's response brief, at paragraph 183. In particular, where he claims to have raised this issue at the 19 July 1993 government session. None of the witnesses who testified about this session mentioned Coric being there and the minutes contain nothing to indicate that he was there. That's P3560. For the more general argument, I would point you to Prosecution's reply, paragraph 129 and 131. Concerning the lex mitior point as the Appeals Chamber held in Dragan Nikolic sentencing appeals judgement at paragraph 81, the principle of lex mitior only applies if a law that binds the international Tribunal is subsequently changed to a more favourable law by which the international Tribunal is also obliged to abide.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, a number of respondents have sought to draw comparisons between our appeal and their respective appeals and claimed that our appeals arguments support their appeals arguments. There is no meaningful parallel between our grounds of appeal and the Defence appeals and our arguments do not support theirs. In terms of compartmentalisation, we've argued that the Chamber erred in law in one discrete area of analysis on JCE 3 liability. We pointed out that the Chamber did not take into consideration plainly relevant findings and evidence because it erroneously considered that these findings and evidence were legally irrelevant to its analysis. There is no analogous Defence appeal. The Prosecution's arguments on compartmentalisation focus on the specific issue of the Chamber's overly restrictive application of the JCE 3 standard. None of the respondents have pointed to a legal error of this nature. Likewise, where we argue that the Chamber made errors of omission, we are pointing to areas where the Chamber neglected to conduct any adjudication, where responsibility for crimes was left wholly unadjudicated or, in the case of ground 3, where the Chamber omitted to enter convictions due to oversight in its cumulative conviction analysis. There is no corresponding Defence argument, and here again our grounds of appeal do not support the Defence appeal arguments. The omissions in the judgement we've pointed to bear no relationship to the Defence claims. The gaps in the adjudication bear no relationship, for example, to Defence arguments that a tangential issue was not discussed to the extent that they would have preferred or that isolated pieces of evidence were not explicitly discussed. In making its factual findings on the existence of the joint criminal enterprise and the intent and the contributions of the respondents, the Chamber considered all of the evidence, including the Defence evidence and the Defence witnesses, making numerous express findings on the credibility and probative value of the parties' evidence. As was clear in the Defence submissions, they disagree with the Trial Chamber's findings, but those findings are reasonable and based on a thorough review of the evidence. Your Honours, if you'll just give me a moment to consult.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I conclude, I have one small housekeeping matter that I would like to address in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go in closed session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: I apologise, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session for a while, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber's findings fell short of recognizing the full scope of the appellants' criminal responsibility. In relation to JCE 3 crimes, the Trial Chamber omitted to enter appropriate convictions for a large number of crimes. And it failed to fully reflect the criminal culpability of the respondents in relation to their superior responsibility and for wanton destruction. The Prosecution requests that these errors be corrected and we ask the Appeals Chamber to ensure that the respondents' full culpability for these grave crimes is properly reflected in the judgements and sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baig, before we move on, Judge Moloto would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Baig, Mr. Sahota this afternoon submitted that the foreseeability test for JCE 3 crimes should be subjective. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, the JCE 3 test has both a subjective and an objective element. Objectively, the crime must be one that is linked to the execution of the common criminal purpose; and subjectively, the accused must -- the accused has to willingly take the risk and the crime must be subjectively foreseeable to that particular accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
