utterances.text: Thank you very much. That, I understand, concludes your submissions in reply. Just for the record, when Mr. Ivetic was addressing us, page 93 of the transcript, between lines 10 and 17, he referred to paragraph and quoted from paragraph 428 of the -- Mr. Sahota, not Mr. Ivetic, from paragraph 428 of the Tadic appeal. In reality I am correcting that. It's from the Brdjanin appeal judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll stand corrected if that is the mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No, no, it is, it is like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: It's a famous quote, though, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but it is the Brdjanin. I know that quite well because it was an appeal from my own judgement so ... thank you. Now we have arrived at the last stage of today's proceedings during which we are allowing ten minutes to each of the appellants to address the Appeals Chamber if they so desire. I'll start with you, Mr. Pusic. Do you wish to address the Appeals Chamber? And you have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not Pusic. Mr. Prlic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRLIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, honourable member of Chamber, [Interpretation] I'll speak in may own language. Instead of the usual words on such occasions, I shall read a part of the text called: We need people of good will, clean hands and pure honour. It's part of the Ramadan rites pushed in a Muslim magazine in 1994: "Considering and emphasizing how war brings misfortune on all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Croats and Serbs alike, Prlic stressed how equal treatment should be ensured for all the citizens. However, to this day, we are not satisfied but we are trying hard to ensure exercise of human rights for everybody. In his own name, and on behalf of the government of Herceg-Bosna, I owe everyone a big apology, said Prlic." What I said at that time during the war I can only repeat now. I am deeply aware of all the victims and all the sacrifices brought upon them by the war. I have spent the war time in probably the hardest places to be then, Mostar and Sarajevo. I know what it means to live without power or water, to be occupied within a city exposed to daily shelling and sniping, left at the mercy of the enemy side and the lack of care from the international community. I have been always aware of everybody's misfortunes even though we were sometimes on different sides. I spent entire years in that area, from 1989 to 2003. 2013 was a crucial year for me. I am aware that judicial truth may not always correspond to the real truth. The two can diverge. But for facts to be contrary to the judicial truth even in this post-truth era is too much. I have been unnerved by this appeal hearing more than by the entire trial and for that I apologise. In the judgement, it seems to transpire that my greatest mistake was not to have left, to have stayed. Maybe it was a mistake. Some people, mainly foreigners, who have changed their minds meanwhile, advised me to leave. But if I had done that, I would have felt guilty my whole life because I would have done nothing to improve the situation. I doubt it that my departure would have benefitted anyone. I remained working there as co-president and then acting president -- acting prime minister of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 and I was one of the first persons who said that it could be an independent state. If you look at the minutes of government meetings during the war and after the war, you can see that there was no interruption in my work, no break from my previous efforts. We had been trying to build a joint state, not a mono-ethnic state, with the support of the international community and in agreement with them. This is confirmed by more than 250 presidential transcripts that we have shown during the trial and in this hearing. Some of them were excerpted in the judgement and they testified to the fact that there was no common criminal purpose. It was just an error in the trial judgement. It was an erroneous finding. After the war, I continued working on building that country all over again, from 1994, first as defence minister, and then as prime minister I represented our country in the outside world for more than five years. And here, the judgement says that I worked against that country and even occupied it for a while. I am aware that the families of victims want someone to be punished, and in this last war we know, all of us, we know more or less who shot at whom. As I said in my interview to the Prosecution in 2001 and as the President Agius said recently, many culprits are still walking our streets freely. I helped and co-operated from the establishment of this Tribunal and continued that co-operation even though a commission was never established. But we have provided a lot of documents and a lot of support, and I cannot resist citing one of them, 1D02243. I participated in many international conferences, and I was representing one of the countries who signed the initial agreement establishing this Tribunal. It's been 13 years since I arrived at the Detention Unit and awaiting judgement. I want to say that the level of injustice in this trial was insufferable. The greatest part of the time I didn't even wish to attend a trial of that kind. At one point I asked I asked the Prosecution to take an oath that they would be telling the truth because they are the only ones who have a mission in this courtroom. This trial is the dark side of international justice that will definitely slow down its development but must not call it into question. If these 13 years were a price to pay for that, then let it be. In any case, these 13 years no one can give back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask your leave to just absent myself for two minutes. I have a medical problem. I need to take some pills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's I understand, Mr. Stojic, that you have decided not to make use of the allowance that -- okay. So it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to say something after all. If you permit. Just for two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. I absolutely support the submissions of my team of attorneys and I would like to thank them for all their work for these many years during these proceedings and I've always had wonderful co-operation from them. I would like to thank them for that.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT STOJIC
utterances.text: I would like to thank the staff for the Detention Unit. Perhaps it is a little bit strange for me to being say this from my position, but I would still like to thank them on a humane and professional attitude towards me throughout the time that I have spent in The Hague. Your Honours, I voluntarily came to The Hague. I believe in this institution. I believe in this Tribunal. And I believe in you, Your Honours, and I am sure that you will reach a just decision in the end. I am very sorry for all the victims of the war, Muslim ones, Serb ones, and in particular, for the Muslim ones, because they were the subject of these proceedings. Thank you very much, Your Honours. That is all that I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. Mr. Praljak. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Last year, the German minister of the interior registered 3700 attacks, including arson, against immigrants received by that state. On average it is ten per day. Dozens upon dozens of powerful state and societal attributes of this great civilised, rich and legally developed country failed to prevent all that. Social psychologists and sociologists have foreseen such events. The foreseeability of the figures is more difficult than to foresee an individual --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but to foresee an individual event is impossible. The number of perpetrators who were detected is minimal. In New Orleans, Hurricane Katrina resulted in hundreds of rapes, burglaries and other crimes committed. The powerful attributes of this powerful country failed to prevent such crimes and the number of perpetrators that was detected was minimal. We know that even small shifts in the social structure may bring about great numbers of individuals who become criminally active. In 1992, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in only a few days, following the Serb aggression, the entire state structure caved in. All state functions collapsed. All the attributes of the state ceased to exist and the state of singularity gained a foothold. One can act in two ways under such circumstances. You can try and keep trying to reconstruct normal channels of authority and the life of a community. It is a difficult task with no promises to be made and excruciatingly slow. The number of killed, wounded, expelled, the number of those who fled, the failed attempts at peace conferences, the betrayal of the Muslim politics, the aggression of the ABiH against Croats, the sheer duration of that war, all of that made those efforts insignificant or devoid of any value. The other modus is acting as an example. I can say for myself that I conducted myself in such a way that now looking back, 13 years later, I still don't know what else I could have done or in what other way. The problem with such type of action amidst chaos has a very small temporal and geographical reach. The methodological error usually turned wrong presumptions or wrong premises is a general occurrence among the western political and social elite. The same goes for these proceedings. Making equal the terms to want to or wish to to the concept of power is something I cannot understand. How come this war was brought about with such consequences if nobody wanted them? And if everybody wanted to prevent them, why then are these power structures so helpless? The degree of efficiency is something called command, control, and communication within the NATO alliance. This concept could be applied to the HVO only if we put the sign of equation between the HVO and the concept of western armies. The sheer content of such terms is far too apart to be compared in any significant element. Such wrong premises make understanding the truth impossible. The aggression by Bosnia and Herzegovina at the front line longer than 2 00 kilometres with the forces of three entire corps, the fierceness of their attacks on the HVO while I was in command placed me and my soldiers at the very edge of our mental and psychological ability and physical ability. Under such circumstances, commanding from the room of a general is impossible. One needs to be in the field 20 hours a day. You have to be with your soldiers, you have to command, you have to motivate and fight alongside them. The amount of frustration among the soldiers also came from the fact that they were attacked by their ally and that everything that ally used in its attack came from the Croatian side. Can it be scientifically foreseen that individuals will commit a crime? Yes. But as to when, where and who is not. In the spring of 1992 and subsequently, as a regular occurrence all HVO members were acquainted with the rules of war. It was done in co-operation with the ICRC. What could we have done to avoid all this? As the Dr. Prlic said, we could have left. We could have surrendered to the ABiH and to the VRS. We could have fled across the border to Croatia, but that would not have reduced the amount of crime. When western alliances fight against the soldiers of ISIS, then collateral damage is unavoidable and it is all taking place. If one does not wish to have collateral victims, do not attack. That's the alternative. To end, in Mostar, the ABiH attacked the HVO. Not the other way around. My participation and my actions during the war boiled down to the Archimedes Praljak theory, if I may say so, and I've read my theorem to the Trial Chamber on the 4th of May, 2009. It is at transcript page 39481 and 39482 of the record. I stand by the validity of that theorem. If ultimately Your Honours conclude that I am guilty, I do not seek for any mitigating circumstances. My conscience is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was born in Croatia. I was not born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it's the same people. Had I -- I was an ex-officer in an ex-army of an ex-state, and I lived for a while in Slovenia, Croatia, and I never lived in Bosnia. I came to Bosnia and Herzegovina in early April 1992, when the Croatian army was getting ready to liberate the southern part of its territory. That part of Croatia is very narrow. Thus, all actions had to be planned along the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the knowledge and approval of Mr. Izetbegovic and the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities. The Croatian army at that time very closely co-operated with the Croatian Defence Council and with some units of the B and H army because they were protecting the left flank of the Croatian army that was advancing. I was not in Bosnia during the war. From July 1991, I had experience of war in Sibenik, in the Republic of Croatia, my home town. Once I came to Bosnia-Herzegovina, I met Mr. Boban and dozens of people who were trying to organise the Croatian Defence Council and put up resistance to the Serb aggression. In view of my professional education and experience, I believed it to be my professional and human duty to help them. I planned, just like we all did, that all that would last for just a few months. However, I remained there for more than two years. Even in the most difficult period of our conflict with the armija in late 1993 I remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina because for me it would have been cowardly and dishonourable to leave my colleagues behind and my soldiers. It would have been the easiest thing to leave, and in that case, I probably would not even have been here today. Still I repeat that for myself, as a professional officer, that would have been treason and abandoning my colleagues and my people in times of trouble. What I would like to tell you today are two things, just two things. First, I really did want the HVO to be an Army of Croats and Muslims and I was really happy about every new soldier. I never paid attention to the ethnicity of any given soldier. In mid-1992, the HVO liberated large swathes of Bosnia and Herzegovina together with certain sections of the B and H army. That was an allied army or, better said, we considered ourselves to be two components of one and the same army. At least that is what I felt. I would just like to mention that in our annex 8, you can see my movements throughout that whole period. But let's take the 18th of April and May. I spent those months, ten or 15 days of each of those months at least, with Sefer Halilovic touring all places that there were conflicts in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So during the two months I spent more time with Halilovic than with my own commanders and we tried to reach every single location. Two, in all commands and contacts I always insisted that the army treats civilians very carefully. When I say "civilians," I mean women, children, and the elderly, which we do not consider to be able-bodied men by law. I issued a series of commands that uncontrolled activities of individuals and groups should be prevented, destruction of houses and other property should be prevented, extremists should be punished, civilian population should be protected in accordance international rules. There are numerous documents that we -- that speak in favour of this. I particularly warned that prisoners, civilians should be treated humanely and afforded the proper protection. I said that civilians had no active role in war and that for that reason they must not be the objects of attack. This is not the occasion for me to point to those documents, Your Honours, but I note that they are in our final submission brief appeal and in the annexes. From my perspective today, it seems to me that I have could acted differently in certain situations. Perhaps I really should have done so. What is certain and what I would not change today is my sincere wish for Croats and Muslims together to defend their homes. Others in Herceg-Bosna also wanted the same thing. That is why we built the HVO as a defensive army. Each brigade comprised men who lived in that area, regardless of whether they were Croats or Muslims. And it was normal for us for Muslims to be the majority in some HVO units. Until June 1993, I did not even believe that this could present a security problem for the HVO. And just a few words to conclude. My Defence, Your Honours, has shown that in 1993, I thought that it's better to negotiate for two years than at that wage war for one day. I think that still today. I think all other people think the same. To see the misfortune that a single shell can inflict upon people is enough to see that war is not the means to resolve problems. However, sooner or later all conflicts end at the negotiating table. It is unfortunate that that is preceded by misfortune and tragedy. I would like to say that I sincerely regret each victim of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am particularly sad about the civilian victims of war, and I hope that nothing like that would ever happen again in that area. Your Honours, thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I may just correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please, just avoid any misunderstand. Page 110, line 21, the sentence is: "I was not in Bosnia during the war." And actually General said: I was not in Bosnia at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we go -- before I ask you, Mr. Coric, can we go into private session for a short while, please. I need to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you've got ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from the moment I was faced with very grave charges before this Court through 13 years of my Hague, I have always searched my soul for an answer: Did I in the past war, consciously or unconsciously or in other way, do any wrong to any person? I carefully listened to all the testimony and read thousands and thousands of documents during the trial. I know there are no faultless people. I know that we, members of the HVO, are also not blameless, but I am convinced that I belong to the overwhelming majority of HVO member who, with the best intentions, honourably and with dignity, risking their lives, defended all the innocent people and their homeland. I hope and I believe that the dishonourable HVO members shall not and cannot tarnish the image created by the vast majority of honourable and honest Croatian defenders. Your Honour, by The Hague indictment some attempted to send a message to me that in the past war I was on the wrong side and part of some criminal enterprise. I would, therefore, like to recall that it is an indisputable historical truth that the most responsible leaders of the Croatian top political echelons, unlike the other parties in the BH, accepted all the solutions and agreements proposed by the international community for Bosnia and Herzegovina, beginning with the Cutileiro Plan through the Vance-Owen Plan, the Washington, and finally the Dayton Peace Accords. It is illogical and unjust that we should be blamed for those solutions that were imposed on us; whereas those responsible are not even mentioned, let alone held culpable. Your Honours, the best indicators of the atrocities of war to which we were exposed is the figure of those dead and wounded in the ranks of the military police. Out of 2.000 of our members in 19 months of war, when I was head of the military police administration, we lost 164 men and had 720 military policeman wounded. If you add to this all the losses in the Ministry of Interior, especially members of the special police and the military police, then the total number of policemen killed is closer to 300 and the number of wounded is over 1.000. Due to huge losses in personnel, we were forced to constantly fill our ranks with new employees. That is why the segment of training new members was a very important one among the tasks of the military police. An integral part of the training was also instruction on Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law and the law on warfare. Because of that approach and the enviable degree of professionalism among our members, many human lives were saved and excellent performance was achieved in combatting and prosecuting illegal activity by criminal groups and individuals. Unfortunately, the fundamental tasks of the military and the civilian police, due to the overwhelming conflict, were frequently put on the back burner despite my continuous warnings. Especially important was the criminal investigations department of our police. In very difficult situations, members of that department in cooperation with other members of the Military Police successfully prevented, arrested and prosecuted offenders for numerous crimes regardless of the army and the people to which the victims and the perpetrators belonged. In that period of war, the Military Police submitted over 2.000 criminal reports to the relevant prosecutor’s office. Your Honours, I carried out my duties as head and minister continuously both inside Herceg-Bosna and in post-Dayton governments of the BH all the way up to 2002. All that time my activity and the activities of my collaborators was always exposed to the public eye and all our public appearances and pronouncements on notorious events were timely, specific, and transparent. In those times, I never planned, incited, ordered, covered up or in any other way participated in any criminal activity. All my actions were directed to lawful and professional action with the emphasis on prevention and combatting crime. I first heard of a joint criminal enterprise from the indictment. I had never been aware of any plan, intent or criminal purpose, nor did anyone ever ask me or suggested to me that I should participate in any such thing. Your Honours, in this courtroom, we have heard over 400 witnesses. Out of all of them, I have not noticed a single professional or personal charge against me. That is why I am surprised that the Prosecutor attempted to present the commendations addressed to me and testimony of witnesses and war-time documents as culpable facts regarding my war-time activities. With all due respect, looking back through the years at all the means used by the Prosecution of this Tribunal in this particular case and some other cases , it is obvious that they have no understanding of the circumstances that prevailed during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecution cannot or wishes not to distinguish what during the war was professionally and humanely possible to do and what was impossible. They do not distinguish between those who fought against ill-fortune of all kinds and working always for the benefit of all from the individuals and groups who acted unlawfully and committed crimes pursuing their personal interests and objectives. In addition to that, the Prosecution used dirty methods and did not stop at striking bargains in order to engage as its collaborators in The Hague proceedings certain lawyers, certain suspicious security service operatives and certain state politicians of the highest rank. These dishonourable individuals, usually from the Croatian people, sold themselves by their false testimony, secret cooperation with the Prosecution and by offering selected war- time documents and forgeries. In this way, the Prosecution consciously amnestied numerous war criminals while being perfectly aware that some of them have committed war crimes, and by covering up criminal activity, they protected criminals and before this Court and other courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they shifted blame onto innocent people. And, finally, permit me two more sentences. Your Honours, I am not a man without faults, nor are HVO members people without faults, but if you have a real perspective of war time events in Bosnia and Herzegovina and compared police indicators of success of a police formation, you will be hard put to find a police unit that was more successful, more professional, and more humane in carrying out its tasks...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]...than the units of the Military Police and members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Regardless of your decision, no matter what it may be, I will always be proud of the fact that during the Homeland War I carried out the duties of the Chief of the Military Police, Minister of the Interior and member of the Presidential Council of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I most sincerely thank all those who have contributed in any way to my war-time activities, and may God forgive all those who made my job more difficult. And, finally, your Honours, I most sincerely regret each victim, especially civilian victims and their suffering caused by this unfortunate war. If I have done anyone any injustice or caused them misfortune during the war, I sincerely beg their forgiveness. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. Counsel for Mr. Pusic, I understand your client has chosen not to make a statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our client has decided not to make a statement. His position is the same as the one he presented in the courtroom in October 1996 when he apologised to all the victims

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he is certain that this Appeals Chamber is going to come to a just ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ibrisimovic. One moment. I need to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Open session].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And at the risk of incurring your wrath, I would like to state for the record that the Prosecution emphatically rejects the serious allegations that were made by Mr. Coric in respect of buying evidence and whatnot. This is a new charge. It's not been made before. And we reject it emphatically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You're not surprising me. I was expecting that. This, ladies and gentlemen, this concludes the hearing of the seven appeals in this case. I'd like to thank, first and foremost, the parties, accused and counsel alike, for their work and their co-operation with the Appeals Chamber. I also wish to express my gratitude to the interpreters, the court reporters, the IT section, and the audio-visual personnel, of course, also the security officers, the Registry staff here in the courtroom, and last, but certainly not least, our staff both inside and outside the courtroom. I must also refer to all other staff members who have been involved in facilitating the hearing during these past two weeks. Thank you all for your very good work and for your assistance. My colleagues and I will now enter the deliberative phase of the appeal, and the Appeals Chamber will render its decision in due course and by November at the latest. The proceedings stand adjourned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.09 p.m.,
